subsubtopic: CRITICISM OF PREMATURE ACTION OF GOVERNMENT RESPECTING PARLIAMENTARY REFORM-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a serious motion to present under the provisions of Standing Order 43. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom):
That this House notes the solemn declaration in the government's position paper on the reform of Parliament, tabled on November 23, that the House of Commons is worthy of more than the cynical cliches, "rubber stamp", "flock of sheep", "trained seals", but that this solemn declaration has been torn up like a scrap of paper by the announcement yesterday that the income tax forms for 1979 have been printed and will be mailed before this House has even voted on Bill C-20, the provisions of which are already in the forms that have been printed and are to be mailed shortly, and that this House registers its strong protest against this blatant contempt of Parliament.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a serious matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the strong expression of community opposition to the development of non-public uses of Cartier Square in Ottawa, in view of the soon to be finalized decisions to be taken by the federal government in this regard, and in view of the fact that no public or community input was sought by the federal government prior to last night, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. McCauley):
That this House supports the request of the residents of Ottawa and instructs the government to freeze for three months all final decisions on Cartier Square in order to allow full public consultation, discussion and input into future land use.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR IMPROVEMENTS TO FACILITATE LENDING CAPABILITIES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, to seek the unanimous consent of the House. As a result of the high
interest rate situation in Canada and restrictions in the Small Loans Act which place limitations on co-operative credit associations and caisses populaires, it is financially impossible for them to lend amounts less than $1,500.
This situation tends to drive the small loan borrower to either borrow more than $1,500, an amount in excess of what he needs, or to seek out other lenders, both scrupulous or unscrupulous, therefore threatening the existence of the co-ops and caisses populaires, the very organizations designed to help the small borrower. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Wightman):
That this House commends the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs for having commenced urgently needed studies of the inadequacies of the Small Loans Act and that it urges the minister and the Minister of Finance to repeal quickly the said Small Loans Act which unduly restricts the lending capabilities of the co-operative credit associations and caisse populaires and, in so restricting them, reduces and even eliminates their inability to provide appropriate lending service to their lenders and small loan borrowers, thus denying needed funds, forcing greater borrowing-

Mr. Speaker, I repeat that I have taken a number of initiatives with respect to the oil supply situation for this winter. subsubtopic: MR. BALDWIN-REQUEST THAT OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT BE DEBATED WITH BILL C-15
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did send Your Honour notice of a question of privilege and I also notified the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Baker), but it seems to me that with a view to a more expeditious and orderly conduct of the business of the House I might well at this time reserve that question of privilege and bring this up as a point of order. It is based on the following circumstances.
On October 18, the House was good enough to pass a motion that a standing committee be established and given

November 29, 1979
Point of Order-Mr. Baldwin
terms of reference to review the terms of the present Official Secrets Act and, inter alia, that no claim of Crown privilege be allowed to limit the extent of the inquiry by the committee. On November 8 1 asked my learned friend, the President of the Privy Council, if he could proceed with the engrossing of a form of motion because it would be very sensible to put this motion together with the second reading of the bill on the freedom of information. Within a day or so I did receive from the President of the Privy Council a proposed draft motion, but it contained no reference to the question of Crown privilege.
I am told that an opinion has been received that it might not have been proper for the House to have passed the motion in the form that it did. This is something that I reject out of hand and it would form the basis of a question of privilege if 1 were to bring it up. If not, I will acknowledge that any motion which passes in this House must be subject to the statute law of Canada, but, in my opinion, when a motion of this kind has been passed, there is no inherent right of prerogative by which Crown privilege can be exercised against a committee of the House. That is something with which we can deal later.
Unfortunately I think the fault may be mine because I was unable to get in touch with my friend the President of the Privy Council to work out the details, and I assume he had his problems as well with his counterparts opposite. However, 1 understand that last night the hon. gentleman indicated that second reading of Bill C-15, the freedom of information act, would commence this evening at eight o'clock. 1 think it would be most sensible for that debate to take place contemporaneously with the debate on the question of the Official Secrets Act. The hon. member said himself that having a freedom of information act without challenging the Official Secrets Act is like flying with only one wing, and I agree with him.
So I hope that between now and eight o'clock, or certainly by no later than tomorrow, something can be worked out so that this motion can be incorporated in terms acceptable to other House leaders, and 1 think I should have some interest in it so that when we commence that debate, we can be debating both these issues at the same time. I know my hon. friend faces the inexorable tyranny of the clock and the calendar; he is learning this problem and he is not being helped too much by hon. members opposite. But I hope that it would be possible and sensible to have both the motion for second reading of the bill and the motion for the establishment of the committee debated together, so that when the committee does receive the bill, it will also receive the terms of reference. I think it would be idle to proceed with one and not the other. So I will leave it at that, reserving the right to bring up the other issue at a later date if necessary.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. This afternoon we have seen that Standing Order 43 can be used to attack the reputation and integrity of an hon. member who cannot reply right away and show how vicious and dishonest these attacks are. In fact, they are moved by intellectuals who know nothing about labour relations and who actually use the rules of the House to show that they are concerned about the workers when in fact they are really interested in finding electoral support.
Mr. Speaker, in the motion introduced under Standing Order 43 by the hon. member for-where does this big dope come from, wait-the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), this lesser hon. member, said, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Longueuil had deliberately insinuated, to have the House and the public believe, that there had been fraud against the workers, against the government and against the credibility of the workers. And I quote from the last part of the motion under Standing Order 43 calling on the hon.
November 29, 1979

member for Longueuil to withdraw his accusations and apologize to the workers for questioning their integrity.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, 1 must remind you that under the provisions of our Standing Orders I asked a question on November 27. It appears at page 1737 of Hansard and anyone who reads it will see that not only did 1 not question the integrity of anybody, but aware that a very good government program was being jeopardized by this kind of accusation-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. OLIVIER-ALLEGED ATTACK BY MEMBER FOR YORKTON-MELVILLE
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member will certainly understand that there is a great difference between a remark made during a debate and a motion. It very often happens that an hon. member moves or tries to move, under Standing Order 43, or any other section of our Standing Orders, a motion containing allegations against another hon. member or a minister, and the minister will always disprove these allegations. And this is exactly the case now, where it can be suggested that the House should debate the terms of the motion. That is one aspect of the problem. If an hon. member, during a debate, puts forward allegations such as these, it is a different matter, but it is very difficult for the Chair to eliminate or reject the ideas put forward in a motion which, after all, must be accepted or refused by the House pursuant to Standing Order 43. Even if the House allows a motion to be put, the ensuing debate or a negative vote by the House have nothing to do with the terms of the motion. A motion must be duly moved by an hon. member to be dealt with by the House. That is the situation in which the House finds itself this afternoon. The hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) was refused the right to put a motion criticizing a minister or the government in general. That is the problem.

subtopic: MR. OLIVIER-ALLEGED ATTACK BY MEMBER FOR YORKTON-MELVILLE
speechtext: I am ready to abide by the Chair's ruling, but I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member-that big dope from Yorkton-Melville-has imputed motives to me, and if on that basis you feel that my question of privilege is founded, then I would like to pursue it.

speechtext: 1 will examine the wording of the motion to see if it is really as reported by the hon. member for Longueuil, because no member may transgress the rules or the precedents of this House either by a motion or by a statement, although it is difficult to prevent such statements made in a motion.

subtopic: MR. OLIVIER-ALLEGED ATTACK BY MEMBER FOR YORKTON-MELVILLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, unfortunately I do not have on hand the motion I proposed under Standing Order 43.

But I am sure that if Mr. Speaker looks at the motion, he will find that there is nothing contrary to the rules of the House. What I said in the motion was very simply that the member could not prove his allegation; therefore, he should not make an allegation and should apologize to the workers because the allegation he made was a bit of a smear against
Privilege-Mr. Olivier
the working people of this country. That is the only thing I said in my motion.
It is no different, as Mr. Speaker said, from many other motions made in the House. In fact, in question period today the hon. members posed similar questions to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Alexander) and the Minister of Labour said, "If you have allegations, make them". He posed a similar question to the Solicitor General and Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Lawrence), if I recall. Again the Solicitor General said that there have been no concrete allegations made and that he knew nothing about it. My motion really indicated that it is fine to make allegations, but if one makes those allegations, please provide the facts and the proof. He did not do that. My motion called upon him to do so, and also called upon him to apologize to the workers.
[ Translation]

subtopic: MR. OLIVIER-ALLEGED ATTACK BY MEMBER FOR YORKTON-MELVILLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand you are going to look into the questions and the motion. But the point is whether the hon. member who introduced the motion used that procedure to impute motives to the hon. member for Longueuil (Mr. Olivier) by virtually accusing him of attacking the integrity of the workers. If you read the two questions put by the hon. member for Longueuil on November 27, 1979, to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Alexander), you will see all the hon. member did was ask the Minister of Labour if he was aware that an investigation had been made by the RCMP as to whether or not funds had been used for labour education. That is not attacking the integrity of workers, quite the contrary, the hon. member for Longueuil was standing up for the workers. As to the question, 1 am getting to it, because 1 do not want to misuse the time you are giving me. I appreciate your courtesy, Mr. Speaker, but when the hon. member uses a motion he may well be in order in introducing it but that does not give him the right to use that procedure to make insinuations, attack the hon. member for Longueuil and impute motives to him. That is contrary to our parliamentary procedure, and to the spirit of Parliament. And I agree with you, Mr. Speaker. You should take time to read the questions of the hon. member for Longueuil, to analyse the conclusions of the motion which are very serious and attack the integrity of the hon. member for Longueuil and indirectly also really attack the workers.
So if someone is doing a poor job in defending the interests of workers in this House, it is not the hon. member for Longueuil, it is the hon. member from the New Democratic Party who introduced this kind of motion which is unacceptable.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. OLIVIER-ALLEGED ATTACK BY MEMBER FOR YORKTON-MELVILLE
speechtext:
Order, please. Members will realize that I have great difficulty in ruling out the text of a motion, particularly when a motion is being put to the House pursuant to Standing Order 43. First of all, it must be accepted by the House with unanimous consent before it can be debated; and then, of course, if it is accepted, it can be debated and refused.

November 29, 1979
Privilege-Mr. Kaplan
Within the application of that rule, it is still necessary to stay within the bounds of parliamentary precedence. But it is quite a different matter to put something of that sort in a motion which is to be debated, than it is to include it in a remark by a member, which in fact is an actual accusation. Nevertheless, 1 still have the obligation to the hon. member to examine the text of the motion to see whether anything contrary to our practices has been done. I will do so and advise the House of my decision tomorrow.
The last notice of a question of privilege which I have is from the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan).

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO NEEDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne included these interesting words:
My ministers were given a mandate to change the direction of the Government of Canada, as we enter the 1980s. The basic purposes of that change will be to enhance the rights, freedoms and opportunities of individual Canadians and re-establish the spirit of partnership and renewal which are fundamental to our Federation.
Further along in the same Speech from the Throne, these words are noted:
To demonstrate the capacity of Parliament, you will be asked to approve the immediate establishment of four select small committees, with the resources and powers necessary to inquire fully into the special needs of handicapped and disabled Canadians; measures to strengthen the role of the voluntary sector in our society-
I presume that the reason I find myself speaking to this motion this afternoon as the first speaker for the government is because new administrations are always enthusiastic about participation and involvement in dealing with long outstanding problems.
No one can deny that the subject matter of the motion before us is one that has been aired from time to time in this Parliament and other places in Canada over the years. As a matter of fact, I introduced the motion on February 23, 1972. As is the time-honoured custom in this House, it was unfortunately talked out. In each successive year there has been a debate, with the same result. I am not unmindful of the fact that historians tell us that from the time an idea is first introduced into Parliament until it is presented and accepted in legislation, usually about 37 years pass. We are doing a little better with the motion that is before us and 1 want to congratulate the new government for making it possible to present it. 1 hope that as members on all sides of the House take part in the discussion this afternoon they will give a positive response and we will have early approval of the motion. As I look around the chamber and see the upturned faces of hon. members who I hope will take part in the discussion, I remember that they have supported us in the past and I am confident that this will be the case today.
While we are proceeding to implement the premise of the motion in a much shorter period than 37 years, I think we

should know at the outset that the history of the rehabilitation movement in Canada covers a longer period of time. I think this is the appropriate moment to make some reference to it.
Actual rehabilitation of disabled citizens, both physically disabled and mentally handicapped Canadians, is a rather modern concept. There was a time when both the physically disabled and mentally handicapped were excluded completely from the community and, in more recent years, provided with a pension. Still, it was a pension and a shrug. The possibility of severely disabled people being integrated into the community and becoming part of the community, usefully employed and making a positive contribution, is a quite recent experience.
It was the tragedies of World War I and World War II that really gave impetus to the concept of rehabilitation. We pay tribute to the work of the Department of Veterans Affairs in this regard, and the continuing work of the Canadian War Amps which introduced for the first time the use of modern technology to ease the lot of the physically disabled with prosthetic or orthopedic aids.
Canada, under the impetus of the tragedy of two world wars, established rehabilitation institutes. These operate right across Canada and provide a comprehensive rehabilitation program, at least for the physically disabled. Our mental health centres, as we now call our mental hospitals, have emphasized returning mentally handicapped citizens into the community with so much success that the populations of these institutions have decreased radically in recent years.
The real work of rehabilitation was done by the voluntary organizations and groups in Canada. There are some 48 voluntary groups that play a positive and useful role in this regard. Obviously they are too numerous to mention but I will mention two. The one in the field of the physically disabled, the Canadian Rehabilitation Council for the Disabled, founded by Dr. Keith Armstrong in the immediate post-war period of World War II, has provided an umbrella under which agencies which work in the field of rehabilitation among the physically disabled have been able to function.
I think the most encouraging aspect of the rehabilitation movement is the recent involvement of the disabled themselves in the program of integration and prevention. The first conference of a new organization was held in Ottawa lask weekend. I am sure many hon. members had a chance to talk to some of the 190 delegates who attended. For the first time we had a coalition of the provincial organizations of the handicapped coming to Ottawa, holding a conference, meeting with members of Parliament and becoming part of the answer to the problem.
This organization of consumers, which calls itself COPOH, is-and let me repeat and underline this-one of the most useful and positive developments in the rehabilitation movement in recent years. They want to solve their own problems and be regarded not as a segregated group but as first-class Canadian citizens with all the rights, opportunities and privileges, as well as responsibilities, of Canadian citizenship.
November 29, 1979

I could spend a long time talking about the work of the voluntary organizations-service clubs, churches, the Chamber of Commerce with its "Employment for the Handicapped" program, and other groups that are now becoming deeply involved in the whole movement of bringing handicapped citizens into the mainstream of Canadian life.
Over the years a multiplicity of policies have been developed on behalf of the disabled. One of the reasons I first became interested in this subject was because of the jungle of confusion and the lack of co-ordination I found in the rehabilitation field. I think it is fair to say that most of the people who are deeply involved in some aspect of the rehabilitation movement are those who have had severe disability within the bosom of their own families. That was certainly my case. As 1 attempted to find solutions, I found that the confusion of red tape, the bureaucratic multiplicity of programs and the lack of co-ordination and co-operation, was a jungle impossible to penetrate.
If hon. members refer to my original motion introduced in 1972, they will see that the idea was to initiate co-operation and co-ordination of the programs and, of course, as we move now toward setting up a formal committee, this will be one of our major functions in dealing with the problem.
Some of the programs are excellent. We have, perhaps, one of the best medical and hospital programs of any country in the world. This led to an emphasis on institutional care, very expensive and sometimes not completely positive, with respect to moving the disabled person back into the community again, so much so that they were often referred to as human warehouses for the chronically ill and the severely disabled. It provided them, as 1 say, with a bed and a pension but little opportunity of moving out beyond the confines of an institutional situation. This program is enormously expensive and yet negative in its results on behalf of the disabled person.
Some of the programs have been excellent, but again not applied evenly. The vocational rehabilitation training program has been one of the more positive programs and most members will be acquainted with its operation. It has become evident that a legislative program is required in order to co-ordinate and bring together the multiplicity of policies and programs, unco-ordinated as they are.
The United Kingdom is moving ahead in this field. On the statute books of the United Kingdom there is an act for the chronically ill and the severely disabled. That act was passed in the early 1970s. The wording of the chronically ill and severely disabled act indicates that already the United Kingdom has moved to bring together those areas of concern for the senior citizens and the severely disabled.
In many respects the problems are similar. We all know that in the next few years Canada's population will be an aging one. It is said that by the end of the century 15 per cent of our population will be over the age of 65. This means that rehabilitation services will be used to a greater extent by a population that is becoming increasingly older. I would think that eventually Canada will have to have a legislative background to
Needs of Handicapped
update its social security programs and its social welfare programs that have grown like Topsy to meet specific needs, much the same as the voluntary associations have grown to deal with specific disabilities, such as deafness, muscular dystrophy, arthritis, mental illness, mental retardation and all the other difficulties to which the human flesh can fall heir.
There has been an attempt to bring about co-ordination in a social services act, as hon. members who have been in previous Parliaments know. An orange paper was presented in 1973. There was elaborate discussion over the years and finally last year the social services act disappeared from the order paper because the method of financing was changed from shared cost to block funding. Therefore, we have to begin from square one again in the very complex program of co-ordinating a legislative program that will bring into focus the contemporary needs of the disabled and chronically ill population in Canada.
I do not want to anticipate what the committee will do but I think that we shall be very much preoccupied with this problem of legislative backup for rehabilitation programs. The committee will come into operation at a very important time in the rehabilitation movement. In the next two years not only in Canada but around the world there is going to be a high profile of interest in the problems of disabled and handicapped peoples.
From June 22 to June 27 next year at the convention centre in the city of Winnipeg, Canada will be hosting the Rehabilitation International Congress which will bring to our shores 6,000 leaders of the rehabilitation movement from around the world. The themes of the congress are prevention and integration and will produce a charter for the 1980s. Already there are committees working on the charter for the '80s which will present guideline parameters within which the rehabilitation movement can operate in all countries of the world. Here is one area upon which the human family can agree.
It is interesting to note that immediately following 1980 there will be an observance of the Year of the Disabled, which observance was approved unanimously by the United Nations in December 1976. Not too many motions receive unanimous approval at the United Nations but here is a humanitarian interest which was approved unanimously. In 1981, flowing out of the Rehabilitation International Congress to be held in Canada in 1980, the Year of the Disabled will bring into focus some of the matters that we will be considering in our committee, certainly issues that will come out of the congress in Winnipeg. They will be tied hopefully to the charter for the 1980s which will be a by-product of the Winnipeg congress. The Year of the Disabled was sponsored at the United Nations initially by Libya. So we cross an interesting number of political differences as we come together to bring into focus the needs of disabled citizens around the world in the year 1981.
The proposal of a committee has stimulated some interesting activities in Canada. Let me just recite a few of them before I conclude my remarks in introducing this motion. Just last spring the Department of National Health and Welfare established a bureau of rehabilitation under the direction of

November 29, 1979
Needs of Handicapped
Andre LeBlanc. The Department of National Health and Welfare, as I have indicated, sponsored the first meeting of COPOH, the consumers group that has come together to resolve its own problems. It is a coalition of the handicapped, not a coalition for the handicapped. That is a vital point of differentiation and these disabled people themselves are bound that they are going to become a vital part of Canadian society.
For the past three days in Ottawa, the Department of Transport has been conducting a hearing on transportation for the handicapped at the Lester Pearson building. The original intention was to conduct hearings over a period of two days on all aspects of transportation for the disabled. There were so many applications to be heard and so many briefs to be presented that it became necessary to extend that conference by one day.
Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, there was a meeting in Los Angeles some two weeks ago. It had international connotations, but Canada was vitally involved in that too through its membership in the International Commission on Technical Aids and housing and transportation for the handicapped. ICTA has been sponsoring resolutions encouraging access to the skies. The meeting in Los Angeles two weeks ago involved major aircraft manufacturing companies in the United States and Europe to ensure that their next generation of jumbo jets will be accessible to the disabled people. Transportation, of course, is absolutely essential if there is going to be any possibility of integration into the community.
Supply and services have also got into the act. They are conducting a study on sheltered workshops. That is a noble idea that came out of World War I but which have tended to be a dead-end street for the disabled. They are a good idea if they are part of the process of bringing disabled citizens back into the community. Supply and services will be conducting this study.
The adult retraining act is being redirected by the Department of Employment and Immigration more to the retraining of disabled Canadians. With regard to human rights, we got our toe in the door two years ago on human rights when employment of the handicapped was included. Last Friday morning the COPOH people met with the Minister of Justice. We now have a commitment from the Minister of Justice and perhaps I should put it on the record because certainly our committee will want to come to grips with this subject. Here is a letter dated November 23 signed by the Hon. Jacques Flynn on this subject:
So that no doubt can be fostered as to the nature of the government's commitment, I would like to reiterate the words of the Prime Minister, as embodied in a letter to the Coalition, from the Leader of the Opposition, on May 1 of this year:
"protection from discriminatory practices should be provided for under the (Canadian) Human Rights Act in a manner consistent with the coverage provided for other protected groups, and we are prepared to amend the existing act to provide for this".
[Mr. Dinsdale.J
Accessibility to public buildings, particularly federal buildings, will be guaranteed by 1983. We still have three years to go on that.
The question of income maintenance is being reviewed at the present time by the parliamentary committee that will look into the subject of pensions as they apply to the needs of the disabled. Sometimes our pension program has introduced a legislative disincentive. If a disabled person was able to earn some income, the pension operated in such a way that the income maintenance program was completely discontinued and the disabled person was not encouraged to continue in the labour market.
These are just a few of the activities that have been stimulated and are under way as a result of the renewed interest in the problems of and policies for the disabled, which in turn has resulted from the motion that we are discussing here today.
I should perhaps refer to the work of the National Research Council which has a special branch dealing with technology for the handicapped. The council is supporting an interesting effort in which I think all hon. members will be interested. In co-operation with the NRC the Canadian Rehabilitation Council for the Disabled, CRCD, has established an agency known as TASH-technical aids and systems for the handicapped-which will make it possible to introduce the sophisticated electronic technology that is now available and make it more readily accessible to the handicapped. This means that totally disabled people, for example those afflicted with muscular dystrophy, will be able to control their immediate environment. Some of them will be able to get back into the work force, particularly those who were professionals, because these environmental electronic controls make it possible for a totally disabled person to handle a typewriter and use the telephone.
I could tell some interesting stories of how this has revitalized the whole lifestyle of some of these chronically and severely disabled persons. Very often in the case of a severe disability, it is sometimes said that you cannot add years to the life but you can certainly add life to the years by using some of this sophisticated technology that is available.
The committee program is outlined before us today, so there is no need to go into it in detail. I think it is important to note that it is a small committee made up of seven. The official opposition and the government will be evenly divided and we will have a representative from the New Democratic Party. I am sure all those serving on the committee will have a personal interest and commitment.
The intent of the committee will be to get in touch with the voluntary sector that I outlined briefly, which is so numerous, and to get into touch with the provinces. Inevitably with any rehabilitation program it is the province that must deliver the services. We will establish close liaison with all government departments and agencies involved in rehabilitation; I understand there are at least 30. It can be seen that our task will not be an easy one.
We will hopefully have attached to our committee, seconded from government departments, as many disabled people as
November 29, 1979

possible. Since the committee was announced, I have been amazed at the number of telephone calls I have received from disabled people who are occupying important positions in various government departments in research, labour, employment and immigration. We have all the talent we need to staff our committee. We will have an additional advantage if we are able to retain the services of some of these disabled people who are highly motivated, sensitive and knowledgeable in the whole field of rehabilitation services.
We want to get as much publicity as possible for the work of the committee. It has been said that perhaps the handicapped person's greatest handicap is our attitude. In recent months some hon. members might have been aware of an information program sponsored jointly by the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Canadian Rehabilitation Council for the Disabled which has used the slogan as its theme "The handicapped's biggest handicap can be your attitude".
We want to use the work of the committee as an educational and informational process so that we might dissipate some of the myths about disability, both the physical disability and the mental handicap. In so doing, we want to assist, accelerate and aid the process of making it possible for disabled Canadians to become a vital part of the community.
We hope to have an interim report in time for the congress in Winnipeg, which would mean in the spring, and in that report will be recommendations for action which can be followed up immediately. Then, as our mandate indicates, we hope to bring in our final report by the end of the year 1980. There have been many studies undertaken, but no attempt has ever been made to bring the information together. This will be the challenge of our committee.
One study-and I close my remarks with this reference- came through with a message which was crystal clear. A questionnaire was sent out to disabled persons, and the response was that they wanted in-into employment, into community living, into maximum participation in community life and into the planning of systems and services designed to help them. At the same time they wanted out-out of institutions, out of dead-end sheltered workshops, out of welfare, out of being pitied and out of being thrust to the sidelines with a pension and a shrug. 1 hope that as a result of the work of our committee we will be able to achieve this desirable goal.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO NEEDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the official opposition welcomes this government's initiative and offers sincere and complete co-operation with this committee. I would like to add my personal words of congratulation to the hon. member who has just spoken for his unstinting efforts on behalf of the handicapped.
However, having said we welcome the initiative, I think it behooves me also to mention one grave reservation we on this side of the House have regarding this initiative. The reservation really stems from the wording of the preamble to this motion when it refers particularly, and I quote, to "the nature
Needs of Handicapped
and scope of current federal policies". If Canadians today know anything at all about the policy of the present federal government, they know that it is one of restraint, and there hangs our reservation.
The previous speaker mentioned that the handicapped of Canada do not want another study. They want into employment, into community living and so forth. Some of the things they want could very well and probably will involve some kind of spending. Some kind of funding is necessary if they are to achieve what they really want. Under those circumstances I think it would be the cruelest injustice and the greatest disservice to the handicapped and disabled people of Canada if this committee, albeit unwittingly but by its very formation, were to raise unrealistic expectations among the handicapped and disabled of Canada.
In other words, 1 think this must be a committee which has some teeth so that we can prove to the people not only that we are listening to them, but also that we do have at least some authority to carry out their legitimate aspirations. If for every legitimate aspiration the handicapped and disabled of Canada tell the committee they have, the committee is to put up its hands in horror and say, "I am sorry, that costs money; the federal government is on a restraint policy, we cannot help," that is the kind of very cruel injustice which I think we should avoid.
As I said, the handicapped and the disabled of Canada need action. They do not need another study. Another study would be a waste of time, and it would be, as I said before, a cruel disservice.
The hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) mentioned that he had started this way back in 1972. I was not around in 1972 to help in his efforts, but I was around in 1975 to help in his efforts and, if I may quote one of my speeches at that time, given on April 21, 1975, as recorded at page 5055 of Hansard, I said;
Some years ago, Mr. Speaker, I was paralysed. It is a sobering thought to realize that if I had been elected at that time it would have been extremely difficult, if not impossible, for me to take my seat, since I could not have manoeuvred my wheelchair into this chamber.
Look where 1 am standing now. If I were in a wheelchair now, I do not think I could manoeuvre it in here.
Indeed, had it not been for the grace of God and the indefatigable efforts of skilled doctors-
People skilled in rehabilitation.
-I would not even have been able to go to the visitors' gallery. On that point, I am saddened to see only three wheelchairs in the gallery today-
Coming back to 1979, I do not see one, but that is irrelevant. What is very relevant is that on April 21, 1975, I said:
We might start putting our own house in order by building a ramp so that the handicapped could visit that gallery, or any others if they want to, without having to perform acrobatics.
That was said in 1975. As I look around the galleries today, I do not see ramps. I heard from press reports the other day that the same situation exists today. I think one of the members of the New Democratic Party was unable to bring some of his constituents to the parliamentary dining room

November 29, 1979
Needs of Handicapped
because there was not sufficient accessibility for them. The situation has not changed. 1 raise this point not so much to point a finger at any one particular agency, or even the House of Commons itself much less, but I raise it to indicate the kind of frustration handicapped people do feel. They hear many people talking about things. They hear many people saying, "You should have this" and "You should have that", but they do not see too much action. We must avoid this kind of frustration in the future.
I am very happy that the hon. member for Brandon-Souris raised the probability that this committee by its very formation would help to create an awareness in the public mind of the very legitimate needs and aspirations of handicapped people.
In that same context I am wondering if perhaps we will not need to define the word "handicapped" or the word "disabled" in order to be able to do justice to the whole question. Incidentally, I am very glad to notice that the terms of reference are very broad. They can encompass very much. I think they can encompass more or less what the committee members themselves want to embrace. However, I think it will be essential to define what "handicapped" and "disabled" mean.
I will give an example. Again back in 1975 as a backbencher and neophyte in the House, I was instrumental in having certain regulations changed as they referred to the Income Tax Act. For instance, effective as of the 1975 taxation year the cost of external breast prostheses could be claimed as medical deductions. Similarly-and I think it was the same taxation year-there was another regulation in which I was also instrumental. Wigs made to order for individuals suffering abnormal hair loss owing to disease, medical treatment or accident would be allowed as medical deductions. The story behind those regulations I think has to surface, and I hope it will surface very clearly when the committee has its meetings. The people to whom I was referring and who benefit most from these regulations are victims of cancer.
Unfortunately very often we "normal" people-who is normal?-think of wigs as frivolous things that we can do with or without. However, the point is that many medical treatments-I am thinking particularly of chemotherapy-do cause tremendous loss of hair. I do not know how long that lasts because I am not a doctor, but there are many medical treatments which do have that effect. That is not a frivolous matter. I do not want to be sexist about it. It is not frivolous for a man, but in the case to which 1 was referring initially it was a disaster for the woman involved because she was a receptionist, and society, being what it is, was not prepared to accept a female receptionist who did not have her hair. It was a tragedy. In other words, it was an obstacle to her finding gainful employment.
It is much the same with a prosthesis after a mastectomy. We are talking about the whole person, the mental health of the patient as well. We can argue as to what society expects women to look like, for instance, but that will not help the

women who, unfortunately, because of a disease or an operation, do not conform to what society expects them to look like. These are the people who are being hurt by society. It so happens that these particular women are victims of cancer. Would they, in the broadest terms of reference of this committee, be considered handicapped or disabled? Not that I want to put them in a category. I will tell hon. members what I want to do for them: I want to save those individuals the embarrassment, the loss of privacy and the loss of dignity that they would have had to undergo to get the Department of National Revenue to recognize that they have a legitimate expense. There is one thing about every human being-and I think it becomes more important when you are disadvantaged for some reason-and that is that human pride and human dignity become much more important when you have lost some of your other faculties. I make no apology for the fact that I want to defend their pride just as much as I want to help them to be productive members of society. These are the kinds of things that we should, in humanity and in fairness, investigate.
1 should like to say a few words about people with impaired hearing. I have been told that they are the largest handicapped group in Canada. However, in 1978 some firm in Kitchener, 1 believe, came up with a new device which converted sound to light. It was a marvellous device for a hard of hearing mother with a new baby, for example. When the baby cries, the sound would turn on a light over the crib and the deaf mother would then know the baby is crying and could go to attend it. If the door bell rings, she can see the light and answer the door. This device, of great benefit to the hard of hearing, became inaccessible to many of them because it was too expensive. In order to get a reduction or an elimination of the federal sales tax, the bureaucracy required is incredible. The firm which had initiated this device had to go through all sorts of departments to prove it would help some people. In the meantime, this device is being made that much less accessible to the very people who need it most. This is the kind of thing I mean when I say we should open up the whole thing. I wish we could have some kind of government department on the lines of class action where, instead of going to every single department of government, there would be just one corner, one counter or one bureau where all these new inventions and all the people who need help can go.
In November of 1976 again I was lucky in acting on a extremely good report put out by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce on the employability of the handicapped. I decided that it should not gather more dust, as so many of those reports do, and that a seminar should be organized on the employability of the handicapped. That seminar was held in November of 1976 in my home city of Toronto. I was very proud that it was held in my city, but what I am not proud of is the fact that that seminar was not repeated in any other centre in Canada. Does that mean that the handicapped of Montreal, of Vancouver, of Winnipeg, or elsewhere, do not need this equal kind of treatment where employers will be made aware of the employability of the handicapped rather than their disadvantage? This is the kind of thing that should
November 29, 1979

be done on a national scale, and not just once because, as the hon. member for Brandon-Souris pointed out, people's attitudes must be changed. You can do so much in changing attitudes if you can educate the public.
To come back to the subject of the employability of the handicapped, I think we are again speaking of awareness and attitudes. I believe the federal public service will have to take a leading role in employment counselling. Our counsellors will have to realize that they must look at the entire person, not just at one facet. They should not adopt a soft approach to counselling but a whole, comprehensive approach so that they can see the whole person, what a person can do rather than the difficulty which that person has. This is absolutely vital when it comes to the counselling of the handicapped who are looking for jobs.
I think the private sector can be very much influenced by what happens in the committee and what happens with its recommendations. I think the Department of Labour in particular could do a great service with many of the studies it is now carrying out. For instance, a study could be done on job satisfaction as it relates to worker productivity. I am sure it would go a long way toward encouraging the private sector to hire more "handicapped" people.
This is especially important in these days of increasing automation. Let me give you an example. Mr. Speaker. In one of the plants in my riding-and 1 have been through it-there is a particular section which is extremely automated. The work there is mind-numbing. At present that work is being carried out by "normal" people who are bored stiff. There is no challenge there. If that same work could at least be offered to the mildly retarded, they would find it challenging and, as a result, productivity would increase. As I said, this kind of thing is particularly relevant in the present climate of increasing automation.
Finally, let me refer to the closing paragraph of the motion before us. I am delighted that the hon. member has mentioned the people we now have around us who happen to be handicapped or disabled. I hope the required "professional, technical, clerical and stenographic help" will, so far as possible, reflect the legitimate aspirations and indisputable abilities of the handicapped. I do not ask for a quota, I ask only for equality.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO NEEDS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO NEEDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1981 has been proclaimed by the United Nations as the year of the disabled. With the striking of this special committee on the needs of the handicapped and the disabled, we are taking what I hope will be a significant step toward substantial Canadian action in an area of concern that is attracting global attention, as societies mature to the point where it is recognized that physical, mental or emotional handicaps should not wipe away an individual's inherent right to live a full life.
The establishment of this special committee can be an important step in ensuring that the special needs of the handicapped and disabled are met, as it has traditionally been
Needs of Handicapped
only through governmental initiative that the quality of life for various disadvantaged groups has been significantly improved. Needless to say, market forces have not been sufficient.
The inadequacy of the current situation in Canada is selfevident. For too long we have been unwilling to permit the disabled to work in many jobs that they are perfectly capable of doing, and to allow them the normal social interaction that would facilitate their integration into normal society. They have instead been hidden away in segregated institutions. This must no longer continue. In fact, the handicapped themselves will not let it continue.
They have begun to defend their humanity, and their aggressiveness in doing so has a lot to do with the existence of this committee. The meeting this last weekend in Ottawa of the Coalition of Provincial Organizations of the Handicapped, and the representations to the Canadian Transport Commission in these last few days, are evidence of what I am talking about. Similarly wc in this House, and particularly the government, will not be spared their righteous anger if good recommendations are ignored-or if the committee turns out to have been a delaying mechanism, a way of putting off action. They have good reason to be cynical about the work of committees and subsequent recommendations, having seen many of them come and go without significant improvement in their situation.
It would be silly to pretend that as a New Democrat I will not be coming to the work of the committee without some preconceived notions of what steps could be taken to improve the Canadian response to the needs of the handicapped and disabled. I keep saying "Canadian" deliberately becaue I think we must ever keep before us the unfortunate fact that as a nation we are far inferior to many other western countries when it comes to our record of action to integrate the disabled into the full life of the community.
As a New Democrat I will be coming to the work of the committee, backed by a resolution passed at our recent national convention which called for, among other things, an amendment of the Canadian Human Rights Act so that handicapped persons could be protected in the areas of services and accommodation, residential and commercial. It called also for direct government action to ensure employment of the disabled by the public service and by those who contract with the Department of Supply and Services.
We must put our own house in order to set an example for the private sector. The federal government, which should be in the vanguard here, has the image of being a very poor employer of mentally and physically handicapped people. The previous government acknowledged this problem in a report presented by the then president of the treasury board, the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Andras). It was entitled: "Government Plans for Increasing Opportunities for Employment of Physical and Mentally Handicapped in the Federal Public Service". However, little if anything has been done, largely due to the restraint policies of the Liberal government.

November 29, 1979
Needs of Handicapped
Employment is crucial to the well-being of the handicapped and disabled. Self-esteem is tied to work in our society. Therefore, employment opportunities are indispensable to the integration and normalcy which the disabled seek. Let us be clear about this. They are not seeking favours or charity, only that their abilities be assessed carefully, that they receive the necessary rehabilitation and training, and that their jobs correspond with their abilities, all of which makes for a situation in which an employer is not getting less for his money but rather a worker as qualified as anybody else to do a particular job.
However, it does not do any good to be qualified and hired for a job if you cannot get to or into the work place. Indeed, if a disabled person were elected to the House of Commons, our experience of this Monday would suggest that such a person would have a difficult time getting into the chamber or into the centre block, through any entrance. Such a person would have difficulty getting into the parliamentary dining room, as was demonstrated on Monday when the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) and myself met with some disabled persons for lunch. They had a difficult time getting in. The tremendous physical, architectural and transportation reform required to realize the goals of the handicapped and the disabled will be expensive, but necessary if we are serious about their needs.
The terms of reference of the committee speak of the need to reflect on the role of the voluntary sector. This is an important task, to ask what they mean by the voluntary sector and what role it ought to play. Too often disabled people, like other groups, have been placed under the well-intended guidance of agencies which sometimes create unwarranted domination over their lives, however much these agencies have done. Certainly everyone would acknowledge the contribution of these agencies and the necessity of the work they have done over the years. Nevertheless, when we talk about the voluntary sector, we must neither forget the necessity of government direction and action nor the fact that in many cases "voluntary" or "private" sector must come to mean self-help and the active participation of the disabled in decisions and policies which affect their lives through support for their own organizations and input into government decision-making. I hope this is an insight which will be reflected in the processes and eventual recommendations of this special committee.
Another problem this special committee will have to live with and seek to solve is the lack of detailed information on the size of the group of people whose needs it is addressing. Information is lacking on the number of handicapped people in Canada, the number employed, by whom and where, etc. We have relied on extrapolating United States data. We must set up a way to gather our own data so that public policy in this country can be guided by what is actually happening in Canada.
This is just the beginning of what I hope will be an extremely fruitful process, and that is the work of the committee. I know the chairman of this committee is earnest about the purposes of this committee. I am also. Whatever the committee suggests will be expensive. 1 hope the setting up of
[Mr. Blaikie.j
this committee by the government is a sign that it regards this area as an area where restraint is not in order, but rather one requiring meaningful and long overdue government spending. Equality, the equal treatment of all human beings for the simple reason that they are human beings and therefore equal to each other, a goal which New Democrats have worked for and continue to work for in other areas as well, will have a price. It is a price I hope the government is prepared to pay.
I know there are many things left unsaid in my remarks. It would be impossible to try to say everything in the time given. For that matter, it would be inappropriate to try to say everything at the beginning of the process. I wanted merely to describe the context in which I see the committee's work. I have much to learn and I look forward to the work of the committee.
In conclusion, I want to say that no amount of legislation by itself will overcome the attitudinal roots of this problem. Discrimination and neglect are as often as not the outcome of fear and stereotyping as they are of deliberate malice. But legislation can and will help as people are put into situations, as a result of legislative actions, where they must come face to face with the inadequacy of their way of looking at and relating to the handicapped and the disabled, as they come face to face with the humanity and abilities of disabled and handicapped persons.
Attitudes can change through direct action and the reality such action imposes upon people. Education alone has never been and never will be enough. It is the non-handicapped and the non-disabled who are the problem. This committee will have to do a lot of listening to those who are handicapped and disabled to be part of the solution.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stan Schellenberger (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO NEEDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to speak very briefly on this subject. I have a few words to say about the establishment of the committee. As members of Parliament, I find that we have the ability to see through many things because we are very deeply touched by people. We represent great numbers of people, and because of that we must at times try to find solutions to their problems. I know that each of us is aware of the many handicapped people who have come to our constituency offices or have met us on the street, bringing forward the problems they have in dealing not only with the federal government, but with the governments of the provinces as well as cities. They have brought forward problems they have as handicapped, a number of which have been mentioned by hon. members who have spoken before me, including difficulties in gaining access to buildings and participating in the active part of our way of life.
1 have a great deal of confidence that the committee, which will be chaired so ably by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale), will be able to go through a number of very adequate studies that have already been carried out. I am sure that committee will be able to relate to the people who come before it with the problems they face, and that the chairman
November 29, 1979

will be able to bring forward recommendations that he and his committee feel it necessary that this House should consider. 1 feel sure that the House will in fact deal with them very quickly and diligently.
A number of people have come to me with problems they have experienced regarding the veterans' acts, the Canada Pension Plan and the Income Tax Act. The committee will have as one of its first problems defining the scope of the disabled so that when we bring forward legislation we will not have problems in the sense of being ombudsmen in our constituencies, having to deal with the situation when constituents come to us with the many problems they have in these areas. In this area the committee will have very important work to do.
I was amazed when looking at some of the statistics regarding the numbers of people afflicted with various handicaps. We who are generally physically able often complain about minor ailments. We really do not have too much to complain about when we consider some of our constituents who do have grave difficulties because of handicaps as a result of accidents or with which they were born. Let me just give very briefly some of the numbers that we are talking about, and these are the 1978 figures.
There are some 15,000 paraplegics in Canada, 13,000 people registered with the National Institute for the Blind, 75,000 Canadians with visual impairments severe enough to cause employment problems, 226,000 Canadians suffering from serious hearing impairments, 50,000 known cases of mental illness, and 250,000 persons treated through outpatient facilities for mental disorders. The committee has responsibility for dealing with a great number of Canadians who must live with disabilities, so the committee has a very important job before it.
I listened with great interest to the speech of the hon. member for York South-Weston (Mrs. Appolloni). One of the things that touched me was the ability of our scientific community to come up with ways to assist these handicapped people in the work they have to do. Yet, as always, we find that we must work through various kinds of forms and make great efforts to get that scientific knowledge to the people who can put it into application. This is the type of thing the committee will have to take into consideration and, hopefully, bring forward recommendations.
It is the right of every handicapped Canadian to live a fruitful, creative and independent life within the context of family and community. This is something we as legislators must never forget. Employment is a great part of every Canadian's life and we must not only provide the financial assistance, but provide the framework within which our disabled and handicapped can find constructive employment. In this way they will be able to perform and get ahead just like any other person who is physically and mentally able.
In 1975 Canada sponsored the declaration of rights for disabled persons which was subsequently adopted by the U.N. General Assembly. That is one of the reasons we are having a conference in Winnipeg in 1980 where discussions will take
Needs of Handicapped
place on the various problems of the handicapped of the world and how we can deal with their problems in legislative ways.
I am sure the committee will be able to bring to the forefront in a way that we as Canadians can all see the belief that the disabled and handicapped are able, given certain legislative measures and the help of the community, to obtain employment and to work their way through the impediments before them. I am sure the House of Commons committee will have an ability in that regard equal to that of any other group.
I am reminded of a Lions Club meeting I attended in my local community. The guest speaker was a lady in a wheelchair who had just competed in the Olympic Games for the Handicapped. We were amazed at the training program she had undergone and the problems she had overcome in order to compete in those games. We were amazed by the ability she showed in the performance of her line of sport. The people in that audience were deeply moved by that experience. They felt after hearing from that person that there were many things they could do to assist in providing more opportunity for the disabled in their communities to participate in recreational activities and sports. That small function convinced the people in that community that there was much they could do to assist the handicapped people.
I am sure there will be much coming out of this committee, but one of the most important things will be the bringing to light by this parliamentary committee of this whole question in a public way, thereby showing the country how the people can assist in helping our many handicapped.
I commend the choice of chairman in the person of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, who has brought this subject before the House many times in the past. I hope I can be of assistance to the committee as it performs its duties in the next year.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO NEEDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like my colleague, I too am very happy that a new committee of the House is being appointed to look into the special needs of the handicapped. After acquainting myself with the terms of reference of the committee, Mr. Speaker, may I be allowed to point out its most important functions. I do hope it will make it a point to insist, first and foremost, on the respect of the individual and not on the differences.
There are a few other areas which this committee should tackle with considerable courage and determination, and which the many committees created in the past did not even touch upon, among others, that of housing. Mr. Speaker, as we already know, the federal government has, through its programs, helped to improve housing across Canada, whether it be public housing, income property or others. I therefore hope this committee will look into the matter and that wherever the federal government invests funds, it will see to it that something is done specifically to help out the handicapped. The same goes for transportation for which the federal government is also making a financial contribution especially for public
1846

November 29, 1979
Needs of Handicapped
transport. In that connection, I think that we could also demand that future investments in that area may enable the handicapped to go anywhere. As the parliamentary secretary mentioned a while ago, we cannot ignore the question of sports which have experienced substantial development in previous years and which, I hope, will continue to receive financial assistance since I feel such an approach to facilitate the integration of the handicapped in the community is one of the best and surest to ensure the quality of life of those individuals.
In the area of education, Mr. Speaker, I hope that provincial jurisdication will be taken into consideration and that our recommendations will be to that effect. I think it would be clumsy for the federal government to intervene in the field of education proper and rehabilitation as far as young handicapped are concerned.
One of the areas in which this committee could play a leading role is that of the public service. In spite of the announcements made in the throne speech and everything we have heard about a reduction in the public service, I feel that a 4.5 per cent objective for the hiring of handicapped employees is both valid and desirable, but that it must be reached over a reasonable period of time. I feel also that this committee should look into the fiscal policy of the government and use every means at its disposal to facilitate the integration of the handicapped in the labour force. While I am aware that a number of handicapped must be exposed to a sheltered type of work, I think that this committee should strive essentially to bring back into the normal stream of life the people who are affected by a handicap instead of making them a special group apart from the rest of society.
On the constitutional level, Mr. Speaker, the committee should make recommendations and make sure that the federal-provincial conferences take into account the important factor of human rights which could be protected if they were already included in the Canadian constitution.
We agree with government members that we must tackle this problem immediately, and I hope the committee will not be only a front for inaction. If that were the case, Mr. Speaker, you can be sure that Liberal members would object to the continuation of the committee's work because I think this committee must lead to concrete action without further delay.
Before resuming my seat, Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw attention to the work rehabilitation programs which already exist and which are going to be cut back because of a cut in funds allocated to Manpower Centres. I spoke yesterday on the phone with the Quebec Manpower Centre and learned that federal funds might be cut back and perhaps even cancelled by next spring, after projects under way are completed. If that is the case, I think the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Atkey) should study this question very carefully, because a committee cannot be created at the same time as funds for the handicapped are being cut.
[Mrs. Hervieux-Payette.)
Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to one of the methods used in Quebec to facilitate the return of the handicapped to the labour force and which has proved rather interesting. I am talking about the famous Canada Works Program. Mr. Speaker, I urge the government to maintain the Canada Works program, a formula known internationally whose past and present merits have been acknowledged. I hope the government will soon approve some projects and pursue this worthy initiative, thus enabling the handicapped to hold a regular job after a training or instruction period. So, I am willing to co-operate with the committee and I hope it will be in a position to recommend concrete measures to the government before its term expires.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO NEEDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased indeed to have the opportunity to speak on this motion because to me it is one that is very timely, particularly in view of the fact the United Nations has passed a resolution with regard to the Year of the Disabled, and also because it is a matter of grave concern to all members of Parliament and Canadians generally. It is one of those issues which cuts across all party lines.
This special committee of the House of Commons will be appointed to inquire into and report upon the special needs of the handicapped and disabled in Canada and the extent to which those needs are being met. 1 congratulate the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) who was really responsible for bringing this matter before the House of Commons once again. I recall that on December 1, 1977, the same hon. member introduced this topic in the form of a private member's motion. He moved that:
-the government should set up a special subcommittee of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, to investigate and report on the needs of Canada's physically and mentally handicapped citizens, in order to provide a basis of information, necessary in avoiding the current costly duplication and overlapping of services, and essential in planning legislation for a comprehensive program of services at the federal, provincial and municipal levels of government-
The hon. member went on to indicate exactly what that Committee should do and how it should be carried out. At that time I had the good fortune to be the parliamentary secretary to the then minister of national health and welfare. 1 stated at that time, and I will restate again because it is fundamentally important in so far as the handicapped are concerned:
Those considered physically handicapped represent a sizeable 10 per cent of the population, and yet, whenever normalization and integration of this group is discussed, two kinds of barriers are mentioned with respect to the physically handicapped, architectural and attiludinal barriers; and for the mentally and socially handicapped, attitudinal barriers. According to a number of professionals in the rehabilitation field, it is really a toss-up as to which kind of barrier is the most important cause preventing the handicapped from full participation in community life. Many of them, in fact, are convinced that attitudinal barriers are the most pervasive kind of negativism. They feel that eradication of these should be a first priority.
I was pleased to hear other members who have spoken today mention the architectural and attitudinal barriers, because
November 29, 1979

they are so fundamentally important. I also stated in that same speech:
It is also necessary to provide these persons with services required to live independently. They might include the following:
1.	Attendant care to permit a disabled person to perform such activities as
dressing and bathing.
2.	Day care services for those who work and have family responsibilities.
3.	Homemaker services.
4.	Meals on wheels.
5.	Recreation services.
6.	Adequate transportation services.
7.	Access to all community services and employment.
All those matters are very, very important to the handicapped and must be considered. It is very important that the committee examine these special needs of the handicapped and disabled in a number of different areas. My time will only allow me to mention a few of these areas. The first is employment opportunities; second, transportation; third, access to public buildings. Statistics are lacking in Canada in so far as employment opportunities for the disabled are concerned. It is important that we get adequate statistics to indicate how many disabled there are, where they are located and how they can be helped.

Needs of Handicapped

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO NEEDS
speechtext:
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to complete my remarks.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. McCain).]
There seems to be a lack of co-ordination in the federal and provincial programs, and even in municipal programs, as far as the handicapped are concerned. There are three departments at least of the federal government that should be involved, namely, the Department of Employment and Immigration, the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Public Service Commission.
I understand that a study was carried out some time ago by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce which indicated that most employers are totally unaware of the proven benefits of hiring handicapped workers, and the handicapped themselves are quite often not aware of the kinds of programs that exist in this country to assist them.
In other countries, such as Germany, France, Italy and England, there is a quota system which, through legislation both in the private and in the public sector, obliges employers to fill a certain percentage of positions with disabled workers. The United States has what they call an affirmative action plan where federal government departments and prospective private contractors are required to fill out forms indicating the numbers of handicapped people that they will be able to use in carrying out a contract.
I conducted a poll in my riding with regard to transportation, Mr. Speaker, and I found that, generally speaking, most people said it was quite adequate. The complaints that I received were basically from the handicapped who said, in effect, that the buses are not adequate, the GO trains are not adequate, the subways are not adequate, and in fact all of the designs that we have in the transportation area do not cater to the handicapped person travelling alone. It seems to me that the only way they can get about is by special buses fitted with special apparatus for the handicapped. This situation is totally inadequate, Mr. Speaker, and must be changed.
The last point I want to make is the question of access to public buildings. A couple of weeks ago there was an item on the news about a reporter who went out to find out what it was like to be a handicapped person. He spent the day in a wheelchair and discovered that carpets in public buildings are a nuisance. He discovered how dangerous curbs are and that most sidewalks do not have a ramp so that the person in the wheelchair can leave the sidewalk and go across the intersection. He also found that opening and closing doors takes tremendous physical effort for people who are handicapped. It requires not only physical strength but mental strength as well. This means, in effect, that public and government buildings must be redesigned and equipped for the handicapped so that the handicapped can play their role in society just like anybody else. We must see to it that the architectural and attitudinal barriers are removed.
I am pleased that there will be a Rehabilitation International Congress held in Winnipeg from June 22 to 27, 1980. I hope I will have an opportunity to attend.
I think Canada is to be congratulated for the measures it is prepared to take on behalf of disabled Canadians. It is my hope that the recommendations and conclusions of the special
November 29, 1979

committee will provide a positive contribution and lead to a step in the right direction with regard to the handicapped.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I think the credo of the Canadian Rehabilitation Council for the Disabled bears repeating: "When you see a disabled person, see a person."
