subsubtopic: CONSUMER AND CORPORATE AFFAIRS-SOFT DRINK BOTTLES
speechtext:
That an order of the House do issue for copies of all socio-economic impact studies carried out by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs in connection with banning returnable soft drink bottles.
She said: Mr. Speaker, on June 28, following reports of injuries caused to consumers by carbonated soft drink bottles which exploded when tipped over or dropped, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Lawrence) announced his intention of regulating, under the Hazardous Products Act "all pressurized glass containers causing bodily harm from flying glass".
The minister at that point requested soft drink manufacturers to stop distribution of, and retailers to remove from sale, the torpedo-shaped, narrow-neck 1.5 litre bottles. In the course of that statement, the minister further said, "I will discuss with the provinces any problems that might be caused by provincial legislation concerning bottles".
On August 7, the minister announced that all 1.5 litre or larger carbonated soft drink bottles, wide-necked as well as narrow-necked, would be regulated under the Hazardous Products Act. He said:
Broader based standards covering other pressurized glass containers are also being developed and will eventually be made operative so that all such containers will have standardized safety tests.
Socio-Economic Impact Studies
On August 28 the minister announced that the ban on all 1.5 litre carbonated soft drink glass bottles would continue until bottle designs provide substantial protection from injury from flying glass. He went on to say:
When such a bottle is developed by using either a plastic film coating or some other means of retention, I intend to propose that the ban be rescinded and that appropriate regulations be introduced for 1.5 litre glass bottles or carbonated non-alcoholic beverages. I also want to make it clear that although 1.5 litre bottles have posed the greatest and most immediate problem, regulations for other sizes of carbonated soft drink bottles will be phased in over a period of time.
Since August 28, the minister has apparently made no further move, and in response to questions in committee said that the ball was in the industry's court, that it was up to the industry to come up with safe containers. But also, even more surprisingly, he said that it was up to the industry to propose the tests against which safety will be measured.
I find this abdication of responsibility on the minister's part very difficult to understand. The minister acted quickly in placing the bottles under the Hazardous Products Act because he considered the matter important from the point of view of public safety. No one would question that the duty of a minister of consumer affairs is indeed to act to protect the public safety. But the minister has been seized of this problem since June and now at the end of November, practically six months later, he is no nearer to offering the consumer clear information on standards.
While soft drinks are not an essential nutritional item, they do find a place in most families' budgets. The consumer who can no longer buy the family size bottle has no assurance from the minister that the smaller bottle is safe either.
The minister has spoken of plastic coated bottles. There is an expensive Japanese technology for plastic coating bottles which is likely to add considerably to the cost of the product, a cost which will eventually pass to the consumer. A Canadian company is developing a technology and has applied to the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Industry (Mr. Huntington) for assistance to develop that process, but we do not know whether the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has consulted his colleague, the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Industry on this matter.
The minister undertook to consult with the provinces. We do not know from the minister what the response has been. The deputy minister of the environment in Ontario has publicly criticized the ban imposed by the minister of consumer affairs; the Quebec minister of the environment has also criticized the ban. The provinces, for environmental reasons and for reasons concerned with energy conservation, prefer the use of returnable glass bottles rather than further use of non-refillables. In fact, Saskatchewan has an absolute ban on the sale of soft drinks in non-returnable bottles.
The bottling industry, which in most cases means small Canadian-owned franchise operations, finds itself with thousands of dollars of unusable inventory of 1.5 litre glass bottles which was used as collateral for bank loans. As the banks call

November 29, 1979
Socio-Economic Impact Studies
in the loans, some of these bottlers go out of business, and more are expected to. The industry has produced figures which emphasize the loss of Canadian jobs, and the minister of state for small businesses has told the industry that he is prepared to be their advocate in government on the issue.
There are always conflicting interests to be reconciled in this kind of decision, but surely the minister has had time since May to collect and evaluate information and do just that. There are questions which must have been asked and answered in his department. For example, is there a difference in safety between new bottles and bottles which have been re-used? If so, has the department been able to arrive at a safe number of times a bottle may be reused? Does the design of the bottle matter? Was there a substantial difference in wide necked and narrow-necked bottles? Would a different method of tempering glass affect shattering one way or the other? Could a safety valve or tap of some kind be used on existing bottles so that the contents would pour out on impact and prevent an explosion? Is the volume of liquid and of gas in the bottle a factor? Would changing this alter the safety factor? With a change in the carbonation process, could safety be increased?
The minister surely must have answers to some of these questions in his department unless, of course, he thinks that all glass containers should be withdrawn in favour of, for example, thermoplastic polyester.
In all thesp choices there are environmental factors and there are cost factors. There is the possibility that in reducing the risk of injury from glass one may be increasing other health risks if the choice is an increased use of plastic. The minister's choice is not easy but his mandate to protect the safety of Canadians is, of course, the overwhelming consideration. Surely consumers are entitled to expect that the minister will indeed make a choice and we will have the reasons for that choice.
The minister has been seized with the problem for five months. He initially began by saying that he would regulate all containers. On November 13 he said in committee that the 750 millilitre container was not dangerous, but this is not what the minister said some months ago, nor has he yet said it publicly. While consumers remain concerned about safety, the industry is concerned about jobs. After six months of inaction the minister can say nothing more but that the ball is in the industry's court.
Since the minister appears to be paralysed by criticisms from the provinces and industry, I would suggest that he make all the background studies available to the House that his department has done. With two former ministers of consumer affairs on this side as well as other interested people, we will be delighted after examining the evidence to help him make his decision.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. M. Gurbin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: CONSUMER AND CORPORATE AFFAIRS-SOFT DRINK BOTTLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to assure the hon. member opposite that the minister is not paralysed but has in fact been working very steadily toward an eventual resolution of this problem, one that I hope will satisfy

both the best interests of the consumers and the bottlers in this country.
I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak about the problems that have been encountered with 1.5 litre carbonated soft drink bottles and to detail the government's course of action in this area.
There are three distinct breakage problems that exist with respect to these bottles. First are the spontaneous explosions. These are associated with bottles fatigued by 20 to 25 trips back and forth from the consumer to the bottler. Second, breakage from being knocked over from the vertical position on to a concrete floor. Third, breakage from being dropped from a height such as might occur on slippage through the hands or falling from a shelf.
The problem is that the flying glass resulting from explosion or breakage can cause serious physical injury. In fact, an analysis prepared by the U.S. government consumer product safety commission in April, 1975, reported that more than 32,000 persons were treated in hospital emergency rooms for injuries related to carbonated soft drink bottles. Long glass fragments and the distances they were propelled were cited as major factors in causing these injuries. In Tel Aviv a shopper reportedly died from injuries received when a 1.5 litre carbonated soft drink bottle spontaneously exploded on a supermarket shelf. And in this country, Mr. Speaker, there have been numerous reports of injuries sustained when such bottles broke or exploded.
Further, in May of this year Professor David Barham of the University of Toronto notified the product safety branch of consumer and corporate affairs of the results of studies he carried out on carbonated soft drink bottles. Professor Barham concluded that the narrow-neck bottles on the market at the time broke and exploded in a violent manner on the first tip when tilted. Because of this alarming evidence of injury, technical assistance was sought from other departments to thoroughly investigate the safety hazard associated with the bottles. I was shocked to learn from our laboratory studies that the bottles dispersed large shards of glass over distances of 20 feet when exploded under the tip test.
The government reviewed 263 complaints received by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and determined that the majority referred to spontaneous explosion and indicated injuries to the eyes, face and arms. In addition, Ontario workmen's compensation board records indicate the bottles were often the cause of injuries from flying glass.
At this point, the product safety branch began putting 1.5 litre bottles through a tip test for regulatory development purposes. The test, very similar to that used by Professor Barham, involved tipping the bottles over on to a vinyl-covered concrete surface. The test revealed that all of the bottles with a torpedo-shaped, narrow-neck design consistently broke on the first impact and projected flying glass with enough force to penetrate the flesh of a chicken carcass suspended in the test area. I would like to assure hon. members that they were not imported chickens. I shudder to think of the effect if a small child rather than a chicken carcass had been the victim.
November 29, 1979

With this negative evidence in hand, Mr. Speaker, we urged the soft-drink industry to remove the narrow-necked bottles from the marketplace, indicating that if voluntary removal did not occur, the department would proceed with regulatory action. Total co-operation was not forthcoming, so consumer and corporate affairs developed a safety standard for all 1.5 litre carbonated soft drink bottles, wide necked as well as narrowed-necked designs.
The standard, based on the best data available at the time, was established under the Hazardous Products Act. It required that glass containers of a capacity of 1.5 litres or larger containing carbonated soft drink pass a tip test. The test for compliance involved tipping the bottles over with a standard measures velocity on to a vinyl-covered concrete surface after they had been allowed to stand unopened and unagitated for two hours at a temperature of 22 degrees Celsius. These conditions simulate events which might occur in a house, apartment or store. Bottles were declared non-complying if randomly selected samples broke and projected flying glass through a four-sided, light-gauge, aluminum foil shield suspended in the test area. In these circumstances their importation, advertising and sale was forbidden.
At the time the standard was established, consumers were urged to return any empty 1.5 litre carbonated soft drink bottles in their possession to local stores in order to facilitate the process of modifying the bottles to provide for compliance with regulatory requirements. At the same time the minister again sought the full co-operation of the industry in clearing the marketplace of the 1.5 litre bottle as rapidly as possible. The response left something to be desired.
But, Mr. Speaker, it soon became obvious that the standard did not ensure complete protection from injury from flying glass under all conditions. A particular bottle design might pass the tip test on one occasion where new bottles were used, and fail it on another where recycled, structurally weakened bottles were used. In effect, the tip test does not fully measure the degree to which bottles become weakened and are made potentially dangerous due to abuse in the recycling process. And because bottles make up to 25 trips there is a long-term risk of physical injury to consumers. Also, 1.5 litre carbonated soft drink bottles have spontaneously exploded on several occasions, and spontaneous explosion, Mr. Speaker, is something that is impossible to control by selective regulation. The control on returnable refillable bottles is not always adequate, as may be seen from their condition on a visit to soft drink displays in major supermarkets.
Because of this shortcoming in the tip test, the minister had no choice but to take more drastic action in order to protect consumers from injury from flying glass, and on August 28, introduced an absolute ban on the importation, advertising and sale of all 1.5 litre carbonated soft drink bottles. Because this outright ban on the importation, advertisement and sale of 1.5 litre carbonated soft drink bottles is viewed by some as a heavy-handed step with potentially severe economic conse-
Socio-Economic Impact Studies
quences for the soft-drink industry, it is important that I stress the safety hazard that has been virtually eliminated pending development of adequate preventive measures.
A 1.5 litre bottle full of soft drink weighs approximately eight pounds, and this weight, coupled with an awkward bottle shape, makes it susceptible to droppage, especially by children or others with small hands. The situation becomes particularly hazardous if the bottle is being removed from the refrigerator and the surface is slippery with moisture due to condensation. On top of that, the height of the bottles relative to their diameter makes them extremely easy to topple-again, a particularly hazardous situation when young children are involved.
During the tests conducted by the product safety branch, shards of glass from exploding bottles penetrated the flesh of a chicken carcass and shredded aluminum foil shields. It does not take much imagination to visualize the effect those shards would have on human flesh, particularly the eye.
Finally on this point, I want to say that in the development of 1.5 litre carbonated soft drink bottles, economic necessity was the mother of invention. The cumbersome design of the narrow-neck bottle allowed bottlers to use existing bottling and washing equipment, and thus save a considerable amount of capital expenditure. Economic considerations may have been the reason for their birth, but consideration for the lives and safety of human beings is the reason for their demise in their present form.
Given that the importation, advertising and sale of 1.5 litre carbonated soft drink bottles in their present form is forbidden under the Hazardous Products Act, soft drink manufacturers are now turning their efforts to the development of a safe container, one that does not spontaneously explode or project flying glass when tipped or dropped.
I do not presume to know the specific design that would be acceptable to the government, but it would probably involve some sort of plastic encapsulation technique for the glass bottle. I understand that a plastic coating on bottles would prevent explosive fragmentation under all the conditions I have just cited and would minimize the possibility of injury should any breakage occur. Unfortunately, officials from both government and industry inform me that time will be required to introduce equipment for the large volume application of coatings. It might also be noted that it is anticipated that such coatings will have the further advantage of extending the useful life of the bottles.
Another possible solution to the problem is the use of plastic bottles. But here arrangements would have to be made with the provinces which are concerned with solid waste disposal and littering problems associated with these designs. If plastic bottles were deemed acceptable, some sort of deposit scheme might have to be introduced to ensure the return of bottles for destruction to avoid ecological problems.
In conjunction with the development of an acceptable alternative to the all-glass 1.5 litre carbonated soft drink bottle, there must be the development of an adequate safety test to

November 29, 1979
Socio-Economic Impact Studies
ensure that bottles in the marketplace are truly safe. As I have mentioned, the tip test has limitations with respect to detection of potential for spontaneous explosion.
Whatever test is finally developed, it will have to simulate spontaneous explosion, which is initiated by a surface flaw. In practice, the source of the flaw is usually rough handling in service and on rare occasions it may be a defect incurred during manufacture. The driving force that expands the crack to critical depth may be a further jarring of the container such as that caused by impacting one bottle against another or by setting a flawed bottle heavily on a counter. Temperature changes may also be the cause; uneven heating or cooling will cause differential expansion of the glass, introducing further stresses and effectively reducing the critical depth necessary for crack propagation and subsequent bottle failure. But whatever the specifics, the critical elements necessary for spontaneous explosion are a surface flaw and a force to drive that flaw to critical depths, and both these elements are provided by the puncture test.
There is full co-operation with the Canadian soft drink industry to develop the requirements necessary properly to evaluate the fragment retention characteristics of flying glass from soft drink bottles.
Now, through the identification of the problem and the development of standards, tests and regulations under the Hazardous Products Act, through the entire process there have been critics who have taken the government to task for failing to properly consult with the parties involved. Nothing could be further from the truth. Officials of consumer and corporate affairs have been in constant touch and communication with the soft drink bottlers and manufacturers, the Canadian Soft Drink Association, provincial ministers, the Retail Council of Canada and U.S. consumer product safety people, to list just a few. At every step along the way all parties concerned have been completely briefed and fully informed. In fact, between May and November there have been no less than 60 meetings with concerned parties.
Let me deal with the question of the submission of a socioeconomic impact analysis of the 1.5 litre carbonated soft drink bottle situation. First of all, when public safety may be in jeopardy it is sometimes important to take immediate and urgent action to prevent or eliminate a known risk. There is no question that all regulatory actions should ideally be based on very extensive and careful advance assessment of their every aspect and potential impact. And I am aware that established procedures for the promulgation of statutory instruments recognize this principle by generally requiring the preparation and consideration of formal socioeconomic impact analyses prior to any major regulatory action. But those same established procedures also recognize that the development of such a detailed analysis can be a lengthy process and that the luxury of prolonged deliberation, in circumstances where human lives and safety are at risk, is not always affordable.
Provision is therefore made for pre-emptive emergency actions to be taken and followed by the required formal analyses. This has been the case with respect to the govern-

ment's action to ban all sales of 1.5 litre soft drink bottles pending product safety improvements.
Also, the ban is simply an interim measure to allow the industry to develop acceptable bottling techniques, and up to this point any analysis would have been a costly procedure that ultimately would have been rendered redundant. However, I can assure the House and the hon. member whose motion is before us that every effort is being made to expedite the completion of the required socioeconomic impact analyses and that they will be tabled at the earliest possible date.
I would point out that these actions would not have been necessary had the industry co-operated fully when the problem was identified.
Throughout my remarks I have tried to emphasize one critical fact, namely that the key issue here is not one of economics, marketing practices or effective bottle design. Those are certainly factors that have to be taken into account, but none of them represents what really counts-an assurance to the Canadian public that the marketplace is a safe place, a place where the products available constitute a minimal hazard to the health and lives of consumers and their families. And surely it is not too much to ask of the Canadian soft drink industry that the products they provide do not break and project flying glass, either from spontaneous explosion or from any type of minimal impact, when the technology is really available.
There is no question that the technology currently exists. I have mentioned plastic coatings as a possible alternative to the all-glass 1.5 litre carbonated soft drink bottle. While there are a few problems associated with plastic encapsulation, they are of a relatively minor nature, and I am sure they can be eliminated if the proper expertise is brought to bear.
I am confident that the application of industry know-how, in conjunction with a spirit of co-operation, will result in the near future in the replacement of a product that was a significant threat to the safety of Canadians. I leave it to the creative imagination of the industry to propose an effective solution.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand there is not much time left before there is a knock on the door here. I want to say at the outset that I support the motion to have the economic impact studies tabled in the House. I support the motion from just one point of view, that is, freedom of information. I think most of the Conservative members would support me when 1 say that we should have as much information made public as possible.
I want to say that I strongly support the action of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Lawrence), and I do not support some of the remarks that were made by the Liberal member who has just spoken. If I understood him correctly, he said that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has created a grave injustice in this country by the banning of bottles. 1 want to say to that member that if the minister had not banned the bottles, he would have created an even graver injustice in the country because of the danger of exploding bottles.
1 want to say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to hon. members here, that it is not just a recent phenomenon that we are talking about here. We have had problems with exploding bottles for a number of years, but the previous government saw fit to do nothing about it.
I should like to quote from an article in the Toronto Star of June 30 this year written by Marilyn Anderson. It reads:
Lawrence Cohen, son of a Montreal restaurant owner, suffered permanent damage to his left eye when a bottle of soft drink he was about to place in a cooler exploded in his hand.
William Hart, a 44-year old Port Colborne bank manager, lost 80 per cent of vision in his right eye, when a soft drink bottle-sitting between two others in a supermarket aisle 12 feet from where he was pushing a shopping cart-exploded.
These are not recent incidents. Cohen was injured by flying pop bottle glass on September 4, 1957; Hart on April 2, 1966.
Both accidents were the result of spontaneous explosions, apparently caused by internal pressure in weakened returnable pop bottles. And, in both cases, the soft drink manufacturer was held responsible and ordered to pay damages.

Cohen was awarded damages of $8,600 in an appeal case before the Supreme Court of Canada on May 23, 1967; Hart won damages of $17,686.66 in an appeal before the Supreme Court of Ontario on March 4, 1968 . ..
In fact, in the ruling on the Cohen case 12 years ago, the Supreme Court of Canada made passing reference to "the numerous decided cases involving the explosion of bottles containing such beverages."
I think it is clear that it was a great injustice in this country not to have had the bottles banned before now. We have all heard the stories of people who sustained eye damage, the stories of the two cases to which I have referred, as well as the case of the little boy in Toronto-I am sure we all remember the case very well-who had his eye actually cut out by glass from an exploding pop bottle. When that type of thing happens, it is imperative that the government of the day defend the consumers against inaction of this sort, and I take off my hat to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs for the decisive way in which he has handled the case.
The multinational corporations which dominate the soft drink industry chose to make a purely economic decision about this evident danger, or so it would appear when one looks at their response. They and some local bottlers had to pay out damages in the occasional court case. Still, these damages would never come close to equalling the cost involved in producing a bottle designed to contain glass fragments should the bottle explode. The large corporations realized something which was repeated, in that same issue of the Toronto Star, by the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), the former minister of consumer and corporate affairs, who is quoted as having stated:
It's irrelevant to say a person can sue a big company, considering the cost and time involved.
I think that is a very enlightened statement when it comes to the ordinary citizen suing a large company, be it Coca-Cola or some of the other large companies involved in the soft drink trade.
The hon. member for Windsor West is something of an old dog and something of an old war horse regarding these matters in this Parliament.

speechtext: What is he, a dog or a horse?

subsubtopic: CONSUMER AND CORPORATE AFFAIRS-SOFT DRINK BOTTLES
speechtext:
Sometimes the most effective hecklers come from one's own party. He is "a rose by any other name."
The hon. member for Windsor West long ago realized that Canadians need legislation like the Hazardous Products Act, plus a large and well equipped staff to administer the act, to protect themselves from members like the hon. member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose), but also from other hazardous products in this country, because, as he said last June "It's more helpful to prevent the injury rather than let the individual fend for himself'.
The present Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is not an old dog in this matter-he is a new person in the portfolio. Indeed, it was quite apparent in the months of June and July that the minister was little more than a pup when it came to situations where he had to handle large corporations motivated entirely by short-term profit considerations. I do not
November 29, 1979

want to describe in detail the first weeks of indecision, but in the words of the hon. member for Mission-Port Moody, all 1 can say is that results of this case show that one can teach an old dog new tricks, or certainly one can teach a new dog some tricks. It is quite a trick for a member of the Conservative party to stand up to the profit motive, when that motive clearly was threatening public safety.
By August 8, 1979, the minister took a step which was requested by the hon. member for Windsor West, the hon. member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), myself, and many others. We had requested that he ban the sale of 1.5 litre pop bottles. As I said before, I commend the Solicitor General and Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs for the decision which he took. I think it was very good and very progressive, and he has stood by it. In answer to a question posed recently by the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. McCauley) in the House, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs rejected out of hand the latest series of merchandising gimmicks which have been the only response from the large soft drink firms to the danger of exploding bottles.
The history of bottle explosions has demonstrated very clearly that the one option which meets safety and environmental concerns is the returnable bottle with a coating or sleeve that contains the glass should the bottle explode. As has been mentioned before, other countries such as Japan and the United Kingdom have developed such containers. It is unfortunate for Canadian bottlers, their employees and consumers, that Coca-Cola, Pepsi-Cola, and their sister corporations would not adopt such a modification in this country until they are forced to do so.
I see some activity at the door to the chamber, but I gather that I have another minute or two. It is very unfortunate that some members of the Liberal party are changing their minds on this issue and have not been standing up for what should be the interests of the consumers. I realize, as I am sure members of the Conservative party realize, that there is some economic hardship suffered by laid-off employees of bottlers. That is real, but surely the fault lies with the dominant corporations which decided that they could lie low, pay off the occasional lawsuit, and haul in profits by sticking with a very dangerous product. I urge the government to investigate the amendment of industrial assistance programs to cover situations such as that which hit the bottling industry, and shield workers from problems which are not of their own making.
Again I congratulate the minister on the tone and content of much of what he has said on this matter since August. I hope he will stick by his guns in making sure that we have legislation which will protect consumers in the future, as he has done to this particular stage. 1 have defended the Conservative party, the Conservative government, the Solicitor General and Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, and everyone for long enough. Perhaps before taking my seat I should say that I find it very difficult to understand the positions of some of the Liberal members in this debate. They seem to be more con-

cerned about protecting Coca-Cola than protecting some of the consumers.
In closing, I should like to say that I support the motion before the House that we make the economic studies public. I have every confidence that those studies will show that the advice the minister acted upon was the correct advice and that he did the right thing. I appeal to my friends in the Conservative party, even though I have defended their action, that they support the Liberal member and the rest of us in this House by saying that it is very important to respect the spirit of freedom of information law, and to make these studies available to the public so that we can have a look at them and decide for ourselves.

speechtext:
that Bill C-15, to extend the present laws of Canada that provide access to information under the control of the Government of Canada and to amend the Canada Evidence Act, the Federal Court Act and the Statutory Instruments Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as I rise to support the principles of this bill, 1 shall not speak very long because there are other hon. members who wish to speak, but I cannot help but think that all of us in this chamber are embarking upon a major reform to our system of government. I hope that reform will make the system better, and I believe it will; that it will be enduring, and I believe it will endure long after all of us in this Parliament are gone, and regardless of what government sits on the treasury benches.
At the outset, Mr. Speaker, I want to pay particular tribute to a member of this House, and that is the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin).

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING ACCESS TO GOVERNMENT RECORDS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING ACCESS TO GOVERNMENT RECORDS
speechtext:
I was given the responsibility by the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark), a responsibility I willingly undertake, to introduce this bill. In terms of the work that has gone on over the years with respect to freedom of information, 1 really believe that the hon. member for Peace River should be standing in my place tonight, introducing this bill. As I stand here to do what is the beginning of the culmination of his work, 1 feel I want to pay him that tribute. 1 feel honoured

to be the beneficiary of the work of the hon. member for Peace River. Members of the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments of this House and the other place, have laboured long and hard over the years to raise public expectations to the point that I can stand in his place to introduce this bill.
If I think of myself as anything, it is not as the father or mother of freedom of information in this country. I am just the midwife of this legislation and I am happy that the hon. member for Peace River is in the House tonight. I expect he takes the view, when he looks at the bill, that the battle for information is not over. I am pleased that he is in this Parliament and will be able to bring his expertise and commitment to the principles that bear on the bill, when it goes to committee.
it was the hon. member for Peace River who commented in this House almost a year and a half ago about the lengthy gestation period for reform such as freedom of information. And, Mr. Speaker, it has been a long time coming, certainly, though, through no fault of that hon. member or of his colleagues in this party. I say that not to be partisan, but to recount what is history.
In that same debate a year and a half ago, the leader of my party made a commitment. He said then it was a matter of urgent priority to present legislation in this House to make it possible for the people of Canada to know what is going on. We have done that. We have done that within months of taking office, but ten years after the hon. member for Peace River first introduced a private member's bill, and ten years after a task force established by the previous government had this to recommend:
The right of Canadians to full, objective, and timely information and the obligation of the state to provide such information about its program and policies be publicly declared and stand as the foundation for the development of new government policies in this field.
It is obvious that the time is overdue for this needed reform. 1 can put the reason for it no more eloquently than did the now right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Trudeau) 15 years ago when he wrote:
Democratic progress requires the ready availability of true and complete information. In this way people can objectively evaluate the government's policies. To act otherwise is to give way to despotic secrecy.
Freedom of information has been studied and restudied by committees of this House. It has been debated and debated again in this chamber. The Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments recommended the concept in 1975. The House of Commons approved it in 1976. In 1977 the former government tabled a green paper which began with these ringing words:
Open government is the basis of democracy. It is an essential consequence of the extension of the franchise of all adult citizens. For a democratic society is one in which the exercise of governmental power is undertaken not by an elite according to its own precepts, but by an executive accountable to the public itself for the goals of government action and the effectiveness of government performance in their achievement.
That green paper was referred, again, to the standing joint committee which found the rest of it did not measure up to the
November 29, 1979

beginning. The committee found fault in both the key elements of any approach to freedom of information; the exemptions were too broad, and there was not an independent review of government denials. The secretary of state of the day rejected the committee's recommendations and never introduced legislation.
But, given that long history, there can be little doubt that members on all sides of this House should have no hesitation about the principle of freedom of information.
In the bill we are discussing tonight, hon. members will not have to go far to find the principles. They are laid out, not in speeches, not in green papers, but in clause 2 of the bill, as follows:
-government information should be available to the public and recognizing that necessary exceptions to the principle should be limited and specific and that the application of those exceptions should be reviewed independently of government.
That clause, Mr. Speaker, will drastically change the relationship between the government and the people it serves. It recognizes that those in authority govern by and with the consent of the people of Canada, not by and for themselves. Nothing can be more important in restoring confidence in government, of whatever stripe, which is so lacking. The reason it is lacking is that governments have been unwilling to take the people into their confidence-to realize it is a partnership, not a one-way street.
Given general agreement on the principles of freedom of information, the task becomes one of turning those principles into legislation. There are, of course, two key elements to such legislation. The first, obviously, is the matter of exemptions from the general right of access. The second is the independent review of governmental denials of access under those exemptions.
To deal with the second issue first, in my opinion it is meaningless to grant broad access to government information, subject to narrowly defined exemptions, without ensuring that refusals to access can be challenged in the courts. Further, it is important that the process of judicial review be as simple, inexpensive, and expeditious as possible.
To allow for complete judicial review, we have taken the major step of eliminating absolute Crown privilege before the courts by repealing section 41 of the Federal Court Act. That section, of course, has always been out of step with the situation in other common law countries. It has allowed ministers to withhold information from the courts in some sensitive areas simply by signing an affidavit. Obviously, retaining such ministerial discretion would eliminate any meaningful judicial review, and the bill addresses that directly.
We have also introduced a step before the court review by proposing an information commissioner with ombudsman-like powers to review government denials of access. This commissioner will have broad powers to investigate complaints and make recommendations. We believe that the commissioner will
Freedom of Information
be able to solve and resolve most disputes between applicants and the government. I hope that belief will be borne out in practice and that we will cut down substantially the number of cases that would wind up in the law courts. 1 would think it unlikely, for example, that a minister would refuse to disclose information if that course is recommended by the commissioner unless that matter is of some high principle which the minister could not avoid. Even if he took that position, that position would be subject to review by the courts.
Let me deal with the other key element of the bill, the exemptions from the general right of access. All those who have examined the issue of freedom of information, and indeed, jurisdictions which have such laws, agree on the need for some exemptions. There is, in other words, some information which should be protected simply so government can function. The question here becomes one of how that can best be done. There are a number of possible approaches ranging from brief, general descriptions of the exemptions, supplemented by regulations as the Americans have done, to detailed and exhaustive attempts at defining the exempt areas. There have been some suggestions that that be done. We have leaned toward the latter. We have tried to lean, in any event, toward the defining of exempt areas using precise language, at least as precise as we could at this stage of the consideration of the bill.
Precise definition will enable Parliament to be specific on what information should be disclosed and what should be withheld. More precise definitions will give more guidance to the courts on the intent of the legislation rather than letting the courts define the exemptions for themselves. Precise, detailed exemptions, although longer, enable the government to define exemptions more narrowly than do broad, general ones. That is the general thrust of the bill.
As I mentioned earlier, while there is general agreement on the need for exemptions, there is much less agreement either in this chamber or elsewhere on exactly what they should be. We have taken the approach that there are four general areas that need protection. First, there are the obligations of government, including such matters of state interest as the conduct of national defence, external affairs, and law enforcement.
Second is the protection of privacy. This recognizes that third parties should not get access to information about individuals held by the government. I might add here that we are now in the final stages of preparing a new privacy act to replace part IV of the Canadian Human Rights Act which controls an individual's access to such information about that individual. The final draft of the bill was approved in the cabinet committee on legislation and house planning this afternoon, and will be going to cabinet next week. It will be introduced in the House before Christmas.
The third area is financial, commercial, scientific, and technical information which could divulge trade secrets and harm the competitive position of commercial enterprises, or interfere with commercial contract negotiations. The last major area is the bill of exemption with respect to the operations of government. That includes information needed for the decision-mak-

November 29, 1979
Freedom of Information
ing process of government, such as cabinet discussions and advice from public servants.
I suspect there is little disagreement that there is a need for protection of information in those general areas, or all of them. This is a question which I know is an open question in the minds of most of us in this House. We have attempted to take a responsible position in answering that question in our exemptions. But when I introduced the bill I was asked what my view of the bill was. I said that I did not regard it as the last word with respect to freedom of information, I regarded it as the first word in terms of this Parliament and that we will be looking to this Parliament, and the committee that will consider it, for assistance with respect to the framework of the bill. I hope that the parliamentary committee will take a hard look at these things. We will certainly consider carefully the recommendations of that committee.
I might also point out, Mr. Speaker, that we have written into this legislation an automatic parliamentary review of its operation within three years of it coming into effect. The parliamentary committee to review the act will be empowered to recommend changes to Parliament. I think it is an important principle that Parliament itself looks at the operations of its own statutes and that the consideration of whether a statute is working appropriately to the convenience of the public and in the interest of the public ought to be left to the representatives of the public. That is a principle that is in this bill.
As important as the principle is that taxpayers are entitled to information gathered by public servants at public expense, the real reason behind the basic theory and purpose of democratic government is that democracy can only flourish with the competition of ideas, argument, and criticism. It depends on the contribution of all voices of society. If this Parliament is to function, if groups in society are to function, if the people of the country are to judge in a knowledgeable way what their government is doing, then some of the tools of power must be shared with the people, and that is the purpose of freedom of information legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to join the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Baker) in paying tribute to the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). Back in 1975 at the request of the then president of the privy council, Mr. Sharp, he and I had the opportunity of visiting the Scandinavian countries to look into the operation of their freedom of information legislation. We spent some
November 29, 1979

time in Sweden, Finland, and Denmark. As well, when we were members of the statutory instruments committee we twice had the opportunity to visit the United States in order to examine the progress that country was making on its revised freedom of information legislation. Perhaps 1 might tell the House a story of what happened to me as a result of visiting Scandinavia with the hon. member for Peace River.
We had with us for the first visit to Sweden an official of the Privy Council whom we had requested to attend with us, keep notes, and write a report on our behalf to the Privy Council. The official was called back to Ottawa as a result of a minor crisis. On his return he produced a report as a result of the first visit to Sweden. He sent copies of that report to the hon. member for Peace River and myself for commentary, and to make sure he had his facts correct. Having got his facts correct, he submitted his report to his masters in the Privy Council.
At that point the hon. member for Peace River and myself went to the Privy Council and said, please release our report, we would like it to be circulated to members of the statutory instruments committee. They said no. After saying no for about six months, we were finally able to get the report out and circulate it to the members.
I went back to the officials of the Privy Council and asked why it had been classified in the first place since two members of Parliament already knew what was in that document. They said that anything produced for the Privy Council automatically had slapped on it a "Confidential" stamp and it took time to be able to undo that.
1 suspect there is a great deal of information within the public service that automatically has a particular stamp slapped on it. It does not have anything to do with whether the information is "Confidential" or "Secret". It has to do a great deal with the way in which public servants see themselves and the normal relations that go on between individuals. It may well be that officials at a certain level will only read documents that are marked "Top Secret", and others read only those marked "Confidential". If you want an input, you have to make sure your documents are stamped with the appropriate top level stamp.
Freedom of information legislation will go a long way toward eliminating some of these problems. At the same time we have to acknowledge that the whole requirement for freedom of information really has to do with human nature, not so much the evil bureaucrats or the civil servants. It has to do with the way in which people see themselves. It has to do with one person saying, "I have information, you do not; so therefore I am more powerful than you." It has to do with the kind of individual games that we all play with each other and which go on in the public service as in any large organization.
The importance of this bill is not so much in the way in which it defines freedom of information and the way it defines exemptions, but the fact that when it is passed it will say that all information should be made available to the citizens of Canada. It is a psychological factor. The importance of this
Freedom of Information
bill is in the psychological impact it ought to have on the public servant.
I commend the President of the Privy Council for bringing to the House tonight the letter from the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) to the public service. I realize that is an important way of seconding the principles implied in this bill. It is important to recognize that all legislation that we pass in this House is of an evolutionary nature. About 85 per cent of the legislation we deal with is amendments to existing acts. That means the government and the people have looked at legislation and decided that it requires improvement. We will have that opportunity to improve in three years after we have a very good look at this legislation.
It is important to recognize that while we may have had differences in judgment as to what should be included in an exemption or in a definition, they are really differences in degree and do not represent major irreparable differences between the various political parties in the House. We are prepared to look upon the legislation, the definitions, exemptions, and even, I might say to the President of the Privy Council, the schedules, which we find somewhat deficient, with the view that it is a question of degree, not of anything else.
One of the most important factors of this bill was not directly alluded to by the President of the Privy Council. This will in fact be one of the major reforms of the public service since Sir Robert Borden's legislation in 1916 when patronage was taken out of the public service. What we are talking about here is in effect changing a system that has grown up over the years in which the public servant has come to be regarded as a servant only of the government, to provide it only with that information and, particularly, to provide it with his knowledgeable opinions and instincts on what a particular issue is all about, in exchange for the fact that his identity will not be revealed. That has been the bargain that has existed.
We have developed a public service which, by and large, is dependent upon the written word. The records of the government are kept in the written word. When we want to go back and check why and upon what evidence a decision was made, we find in the filing cabinets of the bureaucracy the necessary information. That is the way we have operated our public service. We are now changing that. We are now saying that the public servant is no longer directly responsible to the government, that his information was paid for and sponsored by the government which sometimes directed the information gathering and the analysis of that information. This bill says that the public servant is responsible to all Canadians for that information. That is a significant change.
As a result of that change there will be costs to this bill in the way in which the public service acts and in the efficiency of the public service. Just as no piece of legislation is without its faults or its costs, so this one will have costs not only in terms of dollars but also in terms of the way the public service operates. We have to be prepared to acknowledge those costs, to observe what happens in that period of time and to ensure that we are able to find and correct the changes that will inevitably follow. Consequently we have suggested the forma-

November 29, 1979
Freedom of Information
tion of some kind of monitoring agency to investigate the implementation of this legislation. On second thought, we have had to examine it more carefully.
We now propose following the kind of recommendations that flowed from the D'Avignon report, that that function could best be played by the Public Service Commission. It could look at these hidden costs and provide a significant report to the parliamentary committee in three years hence. It is an idea that is worth exploring because of the very nature of what we are dealing with here.
I want to emphasize that this is not only going to be a change for the citizens of Canada, but is going to be a significant change in the public service operations. We have to acknowledge that. As well, we shall have to find some way of protecting the individual public servant. After all, if he goes about his job collecting information and making it available and that information happens to prove embarrassing to somebody-the government, the opposition, individual corporations or others outside government-that individual public servant has to be protected for doing his job. We find that in this bill the individual public servant is not particularly well protected, and we want to ensure that consideration is given by the President of the Privy Council and the committee to ensure that that in fact is the case. We find the bill deficient in that particular instance.
We also find a concern-I do not know what we can do about it-in terms of information flow. I speak of information flow because right now the government really has, in my judgment, three kinds of information flow. We have information flow which is contained in what we might call the standard method of recording, that is, paper documents locked up in filing cabinets and classified according to various methods. That is the kind of information we usually think of.
However, there are two other kinds of information flow which are very important. The first is the question of electronic data processing and the data which is stored on computers. We have dilemmas, and we would want to examine with a great deal of care the way in which the government in the bill has dealt with this particular aspect. We feel that it probably deserves a separate definition of its own and probably separate considerations.
I want, for a moment, to tell the President of the Privy Council of some of the problems we see in this particular area. Let us assume, for example, that the Department of Finance has collected a lot of the data upon which decisions in government are used to make decisions in financial policy and that those data are in the form of a tape in a computer. Suppose I, as a citizen, want access to that data. You give me a tape containing that data. I do not have your kind of computer. The data is no good to me, and it may well be that to have access to that kind of computer is at a cost far beyond my capability. At the same time, if I get a print-out of the kind of data which is likely to be contained on that tape, it would actually be useless to me.
Let us consider also that the government may have some 25 or 30 programs which it runs off that data. Do I request and get a print-out of each one of those programs? Or can I even request the government to give me a print-out of that data using my own programs written on the government's own computer? Yet that may be the only way to use that data properly. So, I would like to ensure that the President of the Privy Council comes to the committee having given some considerable thought to this item. I believe it to be of fundamental importance because I am now told that about 55 per cent of the data which the Government of Canada has, is contained by this kind of information method, which means that unless one has access to considerable computing power, it is absolutely useless. We do not want to end up in a situation where, because the government has converted to a computer system of information storage and retrieval, the legislation itself is worth nothing and is a dead letter. So, I believe that is an important point we want to have followed up in considerable detail.
Another point to make sure that freedom of information is worth while is the matter of indexing. We cannot get the information if we do not know it exists.

That means we really have to pay much more attention, it seems to me, to the question of indexing than is in the bill. I recognize that the government has used the model which was contained in part IV of the Human Rights Act, and I think that as far as that model went it was appropriate because it was dealing with a definable, quantifiable sort of information. What we are now dealing with are all kinds of information which the government has acquired, and therefore we want to ensure that the indexing system which is developed has at least two categories, that it is as comprehensible as we can possibly make it and, second, that it is updated as urgently as possible.
1 also feel that to ensure that Canadians from across the country have access to the government data bank the government must find a means of disseminating this information throughout the land. It is not good enough to say that people can get information only if they come to Ottawa, and in my judgment it is also not good enough to say that people can get data only if they go to an office of which we have perhaps one in each province. I recognize the dilemma in terms of costs, but at the same time I urge the President of the Privy Council to consider utilizing the Post Office again as we have in part IV of the Human Rights Act. I think it is worth considering that. Because of the nature of this country I feel that we cannot keep information exclusive to only one region or to favoured regions. We must, in our legislation and in our actions, make sure it is available to as many people as is humanly possible.
I want to talk at this point about costs. The green paper of 1977 indicated a cost ranging at that time between $10 million and $11 million per year. The paper which was presented by the President of the Privy Council with his legislation indicat-

November 29, 1979

ed a cost of between $5 million and $10 million in today's dollars. We were surprised that the cost of providing information had declined so dramatically in the last four years. We do not think the President of the Privy Council is right in his estimate. We are inclined to this view based on the research which I am aware went into the green paper of 1977, but we are also inclined to this view because the position paper presented by the President of the Privy Council was notably silent on this particular issue. We think the cost will be considerable. We think the cost will be. high, not so much in terms of dollar costs but in terms of the diversion of manpower within the public service.
While freedom of information is a laudable goal, we do not want to see the cost of that borne by the consumers of government programs, and we want to ensure that if indeed costs to develop in terms of the utilization of manpower within the public service, the government will not hesitate to provide the extra man-years necessary to get that information out as expeditiously as possible and not pass the cost on to the consumers of those programs. I think that is of fundamental importance, because to do so is in many ways to take the route which has been taken in the United States. We also think that departments ought to be encouraged to report on a sensible basis what their experiences are with freedom of information.
I have now had an opportunity to review all of the annual reports of all of the departments of the government of the United States since their revised freedom of information act came into effect. I can tell the House that there is absolutely no common system which determines what costs are reported, in what way and how, and if you try to take that material and work out what the costs actually are, it is enough to cause you to tear your hair out. I know that this is so.
When the hon. member for Peace River and I once went to Washington, he and 1 took a separate tour from the rest of the group, and we were told quite frankly that the administration had no interest in finding out what the cost of the legislation was. I think we do have an interest, because it is clear to me that if we do not find out what the costs are and provide for them in our estimates directly, the consumers of programs will pay, and I am not really prepared to see the government taking that route.
I want to deal with one of the points in which the minister took a great deal of pride, and that was the way in which a means of ensuring that a final decision could be taken not by the politicians in Parliament assembled but by the courts of Canada. I beg to differ with the President of the Privy Council. 1 do not particularly think that that is nececessarily a wise move. I accept the fact that no matter in what way we determine the final decision, it is not going to be perfect. My own feeling, as a person who believes in the concept of responsible government, is that it is the government which ought to take the final decision, because in many cases these decisions as to what will be released and what will not will be questions of political judgment, and the government ought to take those decisions, report them to the House of Commons,
Freedom of Information
and then provide an opportunity for the House to be heard on them.
I believe that for the government to go to the courts is for it to take an attitude that it does not feel strong or powerful enough, or have the courage, to deal with the responsibilities it has. I think it is the government that should make political judgments, not the courts, and it is my fear that the cases that will come before the courts will involve as much political judgment as they may involve judicial decision. The judges are trained to make decisions in law. Freedom of information, and the concept of what is contained in those documents which may or may not be released, are better determined by politicians.
I do not lack confidence in the government in the sense that I believe they are perfectly able to discharge their responsibilities. I fear that they will get into a system of judicial decisions which will, in fact, seal off information which ought to be released and keep secret information that is not necessarily secret. So my judgment is that this provision should be looked at again. We feel that the House of Commons has a role to play in this. We are elected by the people, we have confidence in the political process, we even have confidence in the government that they will be able to discharge their duties ably with such a change in the legislation. I recognize that members of the government opposite might not share the confidence 1 have in them, but that is for them to decide.
The last point 1 want to make is to say that, by and large, we are in agreement with the form and the bill. We will be examining very carefully, as will other people, the formulas that have been developed for the exemptions. We recognize that in many cases it is a question of degree and we are prepared to discuss and test those examples that are given in the legislation. We want to emphasize that we believe that this is evolutionary legislation, that this is a good beginning which, by virtue of its very fact, ought to substantiate changes within the public service, that it will be basically a long time in coming to its fruition. By and large we are pleased to support this legislation on second reading.

I want to quote to the President of the Privy Council some words of his leader who spoke in the House of Commons on Wednesday, June 28, 1978. The then leader of the opposition said that there were some criteria in the freedom of information act that he saw must be, in his words, "clear and unequivocal". He is not usually that way, but this is what he said should be in the bill. He said, first, that Canadians have a right to access of information, and the government in turn has an obligation to respect and respond to that citizens' right. Second, he said that any exemptions should be limited and specific, and the burden of proof that an exemption is warranted should rest upon the government and not the citizen. To quote the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) he said:
The law should set forth these exemptions clearly and specifically in limited language and will not be subject or capable of being interpreted in a way that will hide that which should be public.
The third criterion he gave was that there has to be a procedure to resolve disputes over an exemption, an accessible procedure and, to quote him:
[Mr. Waddell.)
-it has to be a procedure in which the final decision rests with the body or a person completely independent of the government that would want to hide the information.
Later he said in a speech:
Any law not based on these principles is a fraud.
I am not saying this bill is fraudulent because it is not-it is a beginning. But if you apply the exacting test of the Prime Minister, it does not quite meet that test. It seems to me that this legislation lacks the toughness, the wholehearted dedication to disclosure which exists in the Watergate-inspired amendments to the United States freedom of information act.
Before I go into the details of where I think the bill falls down, I would like to enunciate some general principles, if I may. We in the NDP, too, want to end our secret society in Canada. In our view, Canada must be the freest country in the world, bar none, and we should never rest until we achieve that objective. The President of the Privy Council has said that the public has a right to know what the government is doing with the taxpayers' money. He put the principle on that level. Let me say with respect that I think this is a rather low way of putting it.
Other people have said that an informed electorate is the truest sort of democracy. That is pretty high sounding. 1 want to define it a little differently, if I may. I would say that the public have a right to know and to have the information which goes into the decisions which affect their lives. Mr. Stevens of The Globe and Mail-that fountain of eastern wisdom-put it this way: that the public has or can obtain information to assess or judge governmental action.
As the matter stands, without freedom of information, many Canadians are disillusioned with government. Who can blame them when governments keep secrets from the people they are elected to serve? The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) gave an example of secrets. I can recall the time when I was up north working for the Berger inquiry in Yellowknife, asking for some material from Ottawa. I received a package which said "confidential-for your eyes only". I opened it up and found a copy of Hansard. It had a speech of Mitchell Sharp's in it. I do not know why anybody would want to keep that confidential.
1 firmly believe that we are talking in a real way about the future of the parliamentary system and the public's confidence in that system. What I have seen so far in this system is that a minister gets up in the House and he or she says, "I have been presented with various options. I have chosen this one", and then the minister sits down. In an ideal parliamentary system it seems to me that we should know what the options were, on what basis they were made, and why the minister chose a particular option. I see the Prime Minister is in the House. I am very pleased he is here tonight because he was a real honest proponent of this legislation. I read all his speeches on it, and I congratulate him for them.

Would it not have been much simpler to make the freedom of information bill, this bill, the whole code? The government does not really scrap, but they sort of scrap them in an indirect manner. This is a government which is trying to inspire an atmosphere of openness. It seems to me there is a big, big mistake in the bill in that area.
Another area about which the government has forgotten, and about which eventually we will get into trouble, is the American experience of reverse information suits. If the government discloses information about an individual or a corporation, the act should indicate that the government must give notice to the person who will be affected by the disclosure of that information. I say this to the President of the Privy Council. We will have law suits over that. We should deal with it now, because we will get into the same problem the Americans had in their reverse freedom of information law suits.
One other area I would specifically like to deal with is the time of the act. It seems to me that if this bill is really to work for journalists, others, and members of Parliament specifically, one needs a tough time limit. That would seem to me to really open up a stalling tactic. Even if they do publish it later on, it seems to me the story or the currency of the information may be gone. (Mr. Waddell.]
Finally in a specific area, l am very concerned with the application of this to the provinces and to dominion-provincial relations. I think we have to look at that exemption very closely. It seems to me that every time we get up in the House of Commons, the Prime Minister or one of his colleagues is always having deep consultation with the provinces, talking to someone in the provinces, and it is a provincial matter, and so on. This seems to be the case in every area. Even our new wonderful Secretary of State and Minister of Communications (Mr. MacDonald) today at the Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts talked about his role in expanding federal-provincial relations for dealing with the provinces. It seems to me we should look very carefully at that exemption." If we are going to have government by federal and provinces together, kind of a new realm of government, then we have to make sure that is a very limited exemption.
From the provinces' point of view, it seems to me if we are going to have this whole freedom of information work, and I know that the President of the Privy Council and Minister of National Revenue wants to make it work, and I am trying to be constructive, although a bit chippy, I think what he should do is write to all the provinces and encourage them to bring in similar acts. It is very important that they bring in such acts. Only New Brunswick really has a half decent act. I wrote to the Premier of British Columbia, but he has a lot of problems with his mail and his letters and I did not get a reply.
1 want to raise one other matter that is important to us as New Democrats. I go back to my definition of freedom of information, and that is that freedom of information should be expanded to the private sector, it seems to me the real Government of Canada, with great respect to the ladies and gentlemen opposite, may not be here. It may be that the Government of Canada is sort of a combination of the government opposite here and the great corporations which plan and meet in their board rooms across Canada, basically in secret. They made decisions which have a tremendous impact on all of us. The great corporations should be accountable because of this impact.
1 am sure some hon. members a few weeks ago saw a report in The Globe and Mail that a one-industry town was closed because a great corporation decided to move. That decision and the information, studies and so on behind it, had tremendous impact on that town, and tremendous impact on all of us. In addition, the great corporations are, to put it not too charitably, right up to the public trough.
Let us take the example of Dome Petroleum which receives subsidies to the extent of 96 cents out of every dollar it spends, and those subsidies are paid by us, the taxpayers, through the government. It seems to me that companies in that position which are making vital decisions, for example, drilling in the Beaufort Sea, should have to make that information available. I am thinking of the studies behind those decisions that affect the Inuit people up there who may want to see those studies. These are important decisions. They are governing decisions, and they are being made every day by small groups in secret.

We have a system, indeed, of private governments in this country. This is powerful and it has an effect on people's lives. If we really believe in democracy, the reality behind that power should be exposed as well. How is this to be done? 1 think it can be done in two ways. These companies or corporations must be required to report to government agencies, to government, and then the information comes under the freedom of information act. They should be required to follow that practice at least to the extent they do in the United States.
The Vancouver Sun had to go to the Securities and Exchange Commission of the United States to find out the salaries of the top executive of the CPR, and other information about the CPR. After we go to the committee, after we pass this bill, and after we hear the words of the President of the Privy Council and Minister of National Revenue, there will be exactly no change. We will still have to go to the United States to get that information. One way to do this, then, is to make our disclosure requirements much more strict and broad.
The second way we could do this is to require of those companies that receive government benefits, advantages, or use the public domain, that they must tell us what they are up to and what they are doing if they want to get that money. This is very important, it seems to me, and I will give you an example. Logging companies are dealing in the public domain, and communication companies have access to public airways. I have already mentioned Dome Petroleum as being one of that kind of heavily subsidized company. In return for being subsidized by the government we should say that they have to live by the freedom of information act, or a similar type of law.
I was not born quite yesterday, and 1 know the government is not going to accept this. I do not expect to see this overnight, but it seems to me that if you accept that philosophy of freedom of information, then ultimately, and it is going to take the Canadian public a few years to come around to it, we will require that from private corporations. This, of course, is the fundamental difference in philosophy between my party and the party opposite. At least we do have fundamental philosophies as opposed to the party on my right.
I would like to conclude by asking this question. Where do we go from here on this particular bill? It seems to me we have to go to committee and do some hard work on the bill. Decisions are not going to get any easier in the future. 1 believe that modern government is going to be very complex. I know a lot of members opposite would like a very simple kind of government, but that is not the way things are going. It is going to be more complex, and technology is more complex now. We are facing a more complex society. In the face of that complexity we do not need the further stumbling block of not having free access to information. In order to solve these problems and deal with this much more complicated world, we need that information.
This bill needs work. I take the minister at his word. I expect a Christmas present from him next week. I take him at his word that this bill is not the last word on freedom of information but, indeed, is the first word. I hope he will accept our amendments, and we will have some detailed amendments
Freedom of Information
to propose in committee. I hope the people of Canada will think about our proposed extension of the principle into the private sector. It seems to me that is what the new democracy is about. Thank you very much.
