Mr. Speaker, I am happy to take part in the debate on Bill C-15, the Freedom of Information Act. Here we are considering another example of a Tory electoral promise embodied in a bill. Of all the promises that were made last year, Mr. Speaker, this one makes the most sense. Data processing and red tape had become tools for controlling and withholding information on individuals. Data banks that can now be found not only in government but also in private organizations and institutions such as hospitals, have grown to the point where they endanger the inalienable rights of individuals to privacy.
So this bill will slow down a threatening process and set up the mechanism that will allow individuals who feel their rights are being encroached upon to have access to those files, under the present rules of the game. Any government information is secret, or at least subject to severe restrictions, unless the minister responsible or the minister in question decides otherwise. I see three points in this bill I want to point out. First, the government and its officials must reveal any information that does not come under an exception in the act. It abolishes section 41 of the Federal Court Act which could be used for all loopholes, and finally, it gives an ombudsman the task of interpreting the law while allowing a right of appeal before the Federal Court.
So this bill, Mr. Speaker, arrives at a time when individuals are concerned with the accumulation of personal files throughout the system. All that accumulated information belongs as much to the individual as to the state. So that information should be available to the individual but, as in any legislation of this kind, that right must be exercised within a specified frame.
The new act eliminates a secular tradition and will not be implemented without clashes. Indeed, undue pressure from individuals to take advantage of the law could complicate the existence of civil servants and the effectiveness of government systems. There is a limit to the non-government information to be released contrary to the U.S. legislation that allows up to a certain extent to obtain information on businesses. Finally, this piece of legislation is only the start of a general process that is to be undertaken. Sooner or later provincial governments will have to respond to that trend and the private sector will not escape it either.
On the whole, we can say that this bill does meet a need that had been felt for a long time. We of the Social Credit Party of

November 29, 1979
Freedom of Information
Canada have always upheld the rights of individuals in their relationships with government. We have always advocated the dignity of the human being and respect for his right to confidentiality. I think this bill will have to be reviewed at some point because it contains exemptions that restrict total access to information. In fact, it is more like access to selective information. It is obvious that for the protection of the collective good, certain information cannot be made available to all.
On the other hand, in this bill, over 50 exemptions limit full access to information. That is quite a few more than in its American counterpart. Though in its own way the Clark government favours the right to information, Canadians will still have fewer possibilities of access than the Americans. Their law stipulates far fewer exceptions to the general principle that government files must be readily and reasonably accessible to the public. For instance, American law allows the FBI to keep its files secret only if communicating the information involved can endanger the life of the individual or cause him irreparable damage. In contrast, the bill before the House allows the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to keep its files secret under the pretext of respecting the act involved. The American law contains a list of seven types of specific information which the Pentagon can keep secret. The bill before us contains some thirty exemptions pertaining to defence and external affairs. Access will also be forbidden to the files dealing with federal-provincial relations. I Find this last restriction regrettable, Mr. Speaker.
I would have liked this information to be available for many reasons of which we are all aware. On the other hand, the legislation contains certain interesting points such as the creation of the position of information commissioner or information ombudsman; the creation of this important position will reduce the problems caused by legal procedures resulting from the present legislation and by the interpretation of this legislation by the courts. Public servants will have to be cautious when they deal with requests for information and they will not be able to interpret the law as they wish because the ombudsman will act as a judge.
The main criticism that can be made about this bill is that it has been too long in coming. 1 wish to thank the government for taking this initiative after 16 years of inaction by the party formerly in power. This bill will be successful if public servants do not resist what they are now required to do and if the public keeps its requests reasonable. It is not easy to implement legislation which pleases everyone, and even though we are in the opposition and our role should be to criticize the legislators, we are aware of this.
It is obvious that implementation of this legislation will mean additional costs for the consumers. We can expect it to cost over $10 million and perhaps $1 million for the information commissioner. This is in fact very little when it is a matter of guaranteeing a right as basic as freedom of information. However, even though a bill may be basically good, we can

still consider making some improvements. In this regard, I deplore the fact that this bill does not consider demanding that Crown corporations such as the CBC and Air Canada provide access to their own files.
However, whatever its weaknesses, this bill will give Canadian citizens official access to information. Until now, personal information was divulged only at the discretion of the government. Confidentiality was ensured by the oath that public servants must take and the often mentioned Official Secrets Act. Reference is often made to the freedom of information act of the United States, but are hon. members aware that Sweden passed an act giving the public access to information in 1766? Until now, only two Canadian provinces, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, have passed such legislation.
Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) for the hard work he has done over the past few years to try and sell the former government the idea of a freedom of information legislation. In June 1977, the Liberal government agreed to introduce a bill on freedom of information. It tabled a green paper on the subject. We all know what happened: the green paper was studied in committee and so abundantly criticized that the bill which the government had planned never saw the light of day.
The new proposal provides for a good number of exemptions, yet it is indeed an improvement over the green paper of the Liberals. I understand the government wants to be careful. No matter how necessary a freedom of information legislation may be, one must not ignore the abuse such a legislation may give rise to. For instance, the American legislation which is famous for being fairly open, has been strongly criticized. One of the criticisms heard more often is the fact that it has been demonstrated over the years that businessmen and criminals are those who benefit most from this legislation, the former by obtaining information on their competitors, and the latter by finding out about law enforcement. I am somewhat worried by this fact, although the intent of this bill is to benefit the ordinary citizen and not the businessman.
This is why the government is acting prudently when it is discharging its duties and the legislation could be extended and altered in a few years on the basis of acquired experience and problems detected during enforcement. At this stage we cannot expect perfect provisions, we need rather a well structured tool to enable us to obtain an acceptable minimum of freedom of information.
By making some criticisms about the bill, I have in no way shown that I disapprove. I merely hope that it will not be final, so the government should undertake to review it in a year or two to enable us to reassess the situation. The bill covers the basic elements of freedom of information and in that sense it is an extension of our Bill of Rights. And since those proposals are relatively new for all neophytes in that area, it is essential
November 29, 1979

that the government do not pressure us to pass the bill. After policy approval, the bill should be referred to a special committee which could hear the various groups involved. It will require much time and patience; however, in the long run we could have a greatly improved bill. In my opinion, the democratic process should not be rushed.

This can be, and will be, the great salvation of this and other democratic countries.
I have been tremendously impressed by the quality of the new members who have come into this House this session, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING ACCESS TO GOVERNMENT RECORDS
speechtext:
When I leave here, as I fully intend to do when this Parliament is over-after another two or three years-this permits me to leave knowing that the country will be in good hands and that there is no obstacle to prevent any hon. member, if he or she has an issue, from taking hold of that issue, fighting for it, finding the facts upon which to base support for it, and presenting that issue over and over again.
The period of gestation of any reform, and particularly of government reform, is lengthy, and difficult. There is nothing that need stop anyone who is anxious to promote a policy or a program. There are no limits to what people can achieve if they want to. Those who do not seek to promote legislative proposals may find other rewards. They may become leader of their party or, even, prime minister. Those are consolation prizes, of course! If one were to go down main street in any small town in Canada-Yonge Street or Granville Street- and say, "Follow me, good and faithful Canadians. We will fight a campaign, we will mount a revolution for freedom of information," one would not get a very great response.
I recently attended a conference with some European parliamentarians who are quite interested in this matter. At first blush, they did not quite see what might be involved in it. I want to say to hon. members, through you, Mr. Speaker, that there is a great deal in it. The democratic world today faces problems in the process of government. I see the Prime Minis-
Freedom of Information
ter (Mr. Clark) here, and I see my other friends in the cabinet here. I know they will agree that this has not been an easy summer, nor an easy fall. The difficulties that we face in this country are the same as those faced in other countries.
One of the problems is that there has developed in the minds of those who are governed, a measure of cynicism and distrust of all of the processes of government. This is by no means justified, but it exists. It is simply not possible to engage in the completion of the democratic process with that state of mind.
Look where you will, Mr. Speaker, governments are changing or being elected with razor-thin majorities. There are situations such as the one with proposition 13 in California. That was not just a matter of people saying they did not like paying so much in taxes. People are thoroughly fed up with the way government has fastened itself upon them and their lives. As proof and substance of this, Mr. Speaker, I offer two incidents.
Last March I went to Washington with a committee which was inquiring into the issues involved in the regulatory process. We met with some of the people in the various regulatory agencies and discussed with them some of the ways they were handling their difficulties. We had discussions with Congressmen about how they sought to oversee the process. It happened at that time that the tragedy of Three Mile Island took place. I was able to watch on television, to hear on the radio and read in the press, the reaction of the regulators and the administrators, of government and of industry. I was appalled by the methods they used and at the language they used. At the beginning everything was fine-all the fail-safe devices were in place and it was represented as a simple problem which would eventually go away. Then the doubts set in, and finally, at the end of four or five days, the governor of the State of Pennsylvania declared a state of emergency. The lies and the cover-up and all the shenanigans which took place inevitably led, some months later, to the great protest when some 200,000 people rallied with Jane Fonda. Maybe she was the attraction which brought some of the people there. This was the inevitable result of what I saw in Washington, however.
This is not the time to engage in a debate on the pros and cons of nuclear power, Mr. Speaker, but that is what happened. There is no doubt that all through the United States and in many parts of Europe there has grown the same distrust of the use of nuclear energy. The Austrians, for instance, have recently established a nuclear power plant in Vienna. Because there was some challenge about its safety, they held a referendum. This might be a lesson to those who are interested in referenda. In any event, 50.3 per cent voted against the use of nuclear power and 49.7 per cent voted in favour of it. The parties were split. The chancellor, a social democrat, was in favour of it as were some of his party members, while others decided to go the other way. In the result, that nuclear power plant was put in mothballs. It will be at least three years from opening even if another plebiscite is passed. I spoke to people from there, to people from government, and to people from the International Atomic Energy Agency. I asked them why. They told me that a campaign was launched and there was so much

November 29, 1979
Freedom of Information
ill-conceived, improper information brought out, that the people were simply disgusted with the whole issue and this was the result of the vote.
I say to the hon. members in this House that this is something we may have to look forward to because, to govern, there must of necessity be some understanding, some sympathy between the governed and the governors. This bill will not be the final answer. This bill will not bring about a millennium. No one bill, no one man on earth, in any event, will ever bring about that millennium, but telling the truth by government will go a long way to restoring the confidence which is so sadly lacking. There is a biblical phrase on which my friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), may correct me if I am wrong-he may even know where it comes from-it is this: the truth will set you free.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING ACCESS TO GOVERNMENT RECORDS
speechtext: I disagree with my hon. friend, whom I like. The truth will set you free. It will set the people free, it will set this Parliament free, and it will set this country free.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING ACCESS TO GOVERNMENT RECORDS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING ACCESS TO GOVERNMENT RECORDS
speechtext:
So it is in that sense that, while I know this bill per se leaves things to be desired, I think it is the breakthrough which will take us a long distance back on the road to recovery.
I extend my congratulations to the Prime Minister and to my good friend the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Baker) and members of the government. I know the task is not easy.
Some years ago, after a somewhat similar struggle the then government followed a proposal which I had made and brought in the Statutory Instruments Act. I remember speaking to John Turner who was at that time the minister of justice. I think some of you have heard of John Turner, his name has been front and centre lately. He introduced the bill which was passed. While the bill was defective in many ways, it was still a mechanism by which this House finally secured the right to scrutinize statutory instruments. I asked John whether he had any trouble with his colleagues getting that bill through. He said, "Colleagues, nothing! My trouble was with the senior officials, to persuade them that this was essential". I am not telling tales out of school. I am sure that my friends in cabinet had that kind of difficulty, that is, to try to persuade people in top level jobs, good people, honest people, people who believe in these views that it was wrong to open up the doors and let fresh air blow through the musty corridors of power. They had quite a measure of success, not as much as I would like.
There are still some clauses in the bill which may need some tailoring, but 1 am heartened by what has been said by hon. members on both sides. I feel that amendments will be passed. I encourage a measure of independent thought on this. I am not revolutionary by nature. There are times when I have achieved a reasonable attempt at being independent. I do not

want to encourage hon. members to depart from party lines, but on issues of this kind when we get into detail, surely there is no better opportunity in an objective way to decide on the question of amendments how we can best bring about some improvement. It will not be perfect. I have long since given up the idea of getting perfection out of this House. We move along and improve.
One of the good things about the bill, is the provision in it for monitoring, for example. It is a considerable breakthrough in the whole principle of legislation, for a government to admit that this legislative child that they have produced may not be perfect. It may have some congenital defects. It is wise to leave to all members of Parliament, both places, who are or must be in close touch with their constituents throughout the country, the challenge to examine the implementation of the bill, and how it is working, to obtain reports from the information commissioner, from the departments and agencies, and to entertain complaints from those people who feel they are not getting an equitable deal, and then, at the end of two or three years, to say, "we will make this report to government", and for the government to say it will accept this report, maybe not in its entirety, or propose amendments.
I have a feeling that if more of that were done in this House that legislation might well be expedited. I do not ever expect to see a complete non-partisan aproach. I would not want to see it. That is not what we are here for. The facts come out better in any situation when both sides are explored. I am an adversary by nature. It is my training in my profession. Any training that I received has certainly been added to in this place.
I think the best way to get at the truth, and the best way to get at the best form of legislative or spending program, is to have two or three sides, maybe even four sides from time to time. But that being the case, there are many opportunities for this House to accelerate this passage of legislation by saying that we admit that something yet remains to be done and we are going to leave to committees of Parliament the opportunity to review what is being proposed and what has taken place under that legislation, and then bring in a report dealing with it. I hope this will be done in other cases.
We are going to deal with the bill in committee. I have a number of amendments but I do not think this is the time for me to bring them up. However, I do want to bring up one or two things which have been raised. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) said that he did not like judicial review. I have been dealing with judges all my life. I have had judges who did things to my clients which I did not think were proper. I did not like those judges nor their decisions either.
On balance, certainly for the first years of operation of legislation of this kind, we must go outside the system. It must be recognized that no minister, no matter how virtuous, honest or decent he or she is, will find the greatest of difficulty arriving at a final, an irreversible decision, which will put within the competence of that minister the right to say that this document shall not be produced, if there is a conception
November 29, 1979

that the document might be embarrassing to the minister, the minister's staff, to the party or to the cabinet. That is very understandable. I appreciate that. 1 think it is going to happen.
Judicial process has worked in the United States. The intervention of the information commissioner here will mean that it will be done only in a very few cases, and ultimately the courts will establish a jurisprudence which will be invoked by the information commissioner. My judgment is that in eight to ten years, which is only a heartbeat in the life of society, we will see that the recommendations of the information commissioner will be accepted in virtually all cases. There will be people in the departments who will know of the decisions and facts, and who will be delighted to disclose the information.
I have talked to public servants. Most public servants favour legislation of this kind. They want to be open. Many have told me, and I have hundreds of letters to demonstrate this, that not only does the public need freedom of information but government departments need freedom of information. They are often incapable of producing the kinds of policies which they should have. They have told me sometimes that they do not know what the minister or deputy minister thinks, or what departmental policy is until they read it in The Globe and Mail or see it on television. Most of them are delighted with legislation of this kind. There are some who hold the reins of power to whom it will not come easy, not because they are wicked or corrupt, but because they are worried about mistakes. There is a saying somewhere that the end product of shielding people from their follies is that you produce a world of fools. That is what can happen in the public service, in life, in our society and in our world.
The cost will not be high. I will not go into that now. I have received figures from my friends in Australia who, in the last few weeks, completed a Senate study of their bill. They sent a committee to America to inquire into their costs. The highest cost in any one year was under $30 million. Relate that to Canada and you look at a very, very small premium struck against expenditures of well over $50 billion. I think for us to put that against $5 million to $10 million, it is a very reasonable premium to pay for the knowledge, safety, and security which go with legislation of this kind.
1 could go on. I will have a chance later because 1 know we will deal with it in committee. I thank hon. members for their support. I thank the government for introducting the bill. I hope it will be passed and passed shortly, within a reasonable amount of time in order to permit the public service to become acquainted with it before it comes into effect. At the end of three years it will be monitored and improved. At the end of four or five years, we will not know that we ever did without it.
People ask me if this will really be used. I practised law for a great many years before 1 was seduced into politics. In all the years I practised, I only prepared papers for habeas corpus three times. Habeas corpus is the rule by which you have the body before the court to justify the imprisonment. The very fact that the writ of habeas corpus exists has constituted a
Freedom of Information
wholesome safeguard and restraint upon abuses by public authorities in the confinement of individual citizens. We will change to habeaus documentus. Is that good Latin? The very fact the law exists will contitute a wholesome and healthy restraint on the extent to which governments fail to disclose the business of the country to the people. It is a good law. It will be improved and become a better law. I commend it to hon. members of this House, the public service, and the country.

subtopic: FORESTRY-ACTION TAKEN TO PROTECT INDUSTRY-FUNDS FOR EXPANSION OF PULP MILLS
FORESTRY-ACTION TAKEN TO PROTECT INDUSTRY-FUNDS FOR EXPANSION OF PULP MILLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I sense an air in the House this evening with which I want to associate myself. That is with respect to the quick passage at second reading of Bill C-15. I support any steps which might be taken by the government with respect to freedom of information.
I agree that it is important on such matters that there be non-partisan debate, and as 1 get on to my topic with respect to forestry, I want to relieve you, Mr. Speaker, of any anxiety by telling the House that I place an equal amount of importance on the topic to which I will address myself this evening, that being the ever-present importance of the planning and full development of that rich natural resource in Canada, forestry.
In my work with the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs in the last session there were non-partisan efforts to bring forward penal reform. In that joint report there was full support from all sides of the House on penal reform. That is an example of what can be done when men and women have the will to work together. I certainly feel that that approach is important in this House.
My reason for participating in this debate at this time is the result of what has to be termed a non-answer by the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Wilson) when, some days ago, I posed a question to him in the question period as to what he could tell the House about what the government's position would be, or is today, with respect to all aspects of forestry planning, the financing of future development of this industry, reforestation, the whole question of the environment, and the effect which acid rain will have on this rich resource.
Of course, it will be quickly observed that I was disappointed and not very satisfied with the minister's response. I pointed out to him that the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) and the government of the day had missed a golden opportunity to include this all-important subject to all Canadians in the Speech from the Throne and to give us at least a glimpse or an idea of where they stood on this important topic. They missed a golden opportunity to tell us what they had in mind and what their plans would l>e regarding the short-term and long-term effects of this industry. I mentioned at the time that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. de Cotret) who, of course, has direct responsibility, does not enjoy the pleasure of residing in this House. He is in the other place, and as a result 1 had to put my question to the Minister of State for International Trade.
I asked the minister what his government's position was, what the plans were for the future of this important natural resource, and what the government intended to do, in view of the fact that it did not see fit to include it anywhere in the Speech from the Throne. No reference was made to it in the Speech from the Throne, which was the government's golden opportunity to set forth its plans for the future of this industry. Of course, in his total non-answer he advised the House he would take the question as notice and get back to us. There is only one word for that. It is astonishing that the man who has

November 29, 1979

responsibility for international trade would inform the House that he would look into the matter and get back to the House.
This industry represents something in excess of $3 billion in revenues to the country. It represents in excess of 29 per cent of our international trade, and the Minister of State for International Trade tells the House that he has not really sorted it out in his own mind yet. He leaves it to us to interpret, as we must, because he said, "I don't know; I will look into it and get back to you". That is the reason for my having to return this evening by way of the adjournment debate to stress this matter once again.
I do not think that in a democracy we should have to plead with the government. The Prime Minister has a responsibility at least to co-ordinate the cabinet committee, to discuss with the Minister of Finance (Mr Crosbie), the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens), the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Fraser), the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Minister of State for International Trade, and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Alexander) and to decide on what exactly their strategy and what their plan to protect the future of this all-important natural resource will be.
We know that there are problems in this industry with respect to supply. Many of the large international corporations, such as Canadian International Paper, many of the Canadian companies in British Columbia and in the Atlantic area, are concerned with the whole question of supply. How can you expect these captains of industry to consider reinvesting millions of dollars if they do not have some indication from the government of support, aid, and planning for the future to give them some guarantee of supply in the future?
I do not expect for a moment that any member of any side of the House would disagree with me as to the importance of the planning and protection of this industry. Certainly the Minister of the Environment, who is from British Columbia, is concerned with the protection of this important resource. But the more important resource, namely, the people of this country, the question of jobs and employment, the protection of people who work in pulp and paper mills, people who work in the woods industry from Newfoundland to Vancouver, should be sufficient evidence to convince the government of the day that it must take a serious view, that it must seriously consider this question and that it must inform the House and Canadians on exactly what its position is and what it intends to do in the future. I call upon ministers to do that.

speakeroldname: Mr. Richard Janelie (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subtopic: FORESTRY-ACTION TAKEN TO PROTECT INDUSTRY-FUNDS FOR EXPANSION OF PULP MILLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to tell the hon. member that the government is not only actively engaged in providing direct assistance to the pulp and paper industry but also involved in the development and scientific management of forest resources.
Under the national program for the development of the forest product industry, financial help is available to promote
Adjournment Debate
the modernization of operations concerning wood products as well as conservation measures and the development of the forest resources of the nation. Other measures and other programs are also available such as the renewable energy program of the forest industry, accrued tax credits, and the extension of the accelerated depreciation allowance for equipment designed to control pollution. All these programs are part of a rather comprehensive package of assistance provided by the federal government.
In all these other programs, my colleagues, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn), the Minister of Environment (Mr. Fraser) through the Canadian Forestry Service, and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, (Mr. de Cotret) are all actively involved in promoting this vital industry of the Canadian economy.
We offer financial assistance to the forest products industry to encourage corporations to invest in projects they would not venture into if they were to fend for themselves. A certain number of grants have already been approved to prompt companies to undertake various modernization projects, Spruce Falls among others, and several other projects are being considered by the industry itself or by governmental agencies. As far as forest resources themselves are concerned, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has negotiated and signed subsidiary agreements with seven provinces to ensure long-term stability for one of our most important renewable resources. We have taken this action on a cost-sharing basis with the provinces, which have given high priority to the development of this resource. 1 must also add that the Canadian Forestry Service offers a wide variety of services to this important industrial sector through various scientific and research management activities.
I would also, with pleasure, give my hon. colleague a recently prepared internal document which outlines the commitment of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion in the field of forest products, including its contribution under the Regional Development Incentives Act. I trust this will satisfy the hon. member, and should further questions come to his mind, the ministers responsible will be pleased to answer him.

subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-SALE OF NORDAIR-INQUIRY WHETHER QUESTION WILL BE REFERRED TO CTC
AIR TRANSPORT-SALE OF NORDAIR-INQUIRY WHETHER QUESTION WILL BE REFERRED TO CTC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 24 last, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) indicated to the House and the Canadian people that he intended to make a recommendation to cabinet on the sale of Nordair, and further to ensure, and I quote:
That this will have to be approved by the CTC in due course.
My supplementary reminded the Minister of Transport that the CTC has exclusive authority in this matter, and the

November 29, 1979
Adjournment Debate
minister answered the government had no intention of impos ing a political decision on an administrative court.
With all due respect, I submit his actions point to the contrary, and it is exactly a political decision he wants to impose on the CTC, an administrative court.
The CTC's decisions are subject to appeal to the Privy Council, among others. This is a form of review after the fact that is the rule in this party when administrative courts are involved. Unfortunately, such is not the case with our Progressive Conservative friends who wish to impose their political will on the Canadian Transport Commission even before it is involved with the case.
The President of the Canadian Transport Commission indicated to me, at the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, in answer to one of my questions, as reported on page 4.26, and 1 quote:
If the government. .. want to pass an order in council saying, we are going to sell Nordair to so-and-so, I think we would find it very difficult to say no, because if we said no, it would be appealed back to the cabinet and they would say yes.
Clearly, Mr. Speaker, the commission is quite powerless under the circumstances. It is even embarrassed that the Progressive Conservatives are questioning its integrity and objectivity.
Mr. Speaker, some decisions made by organizations responsible to Parliament may be reviewed by the governor in council or a minister. It is especially true for decisions made by the Canadian Transport Commission. This control can take the form of an appeal, an approval, a cancellation, or a revision at the request of one of the parties or on the initiative of the political jurisdiction. A posteriori control would allow the cabinet to change or rescind a decision made by the Canadian Transport Commission if there was, of course, serious reasons to do it.
The surveillance and control power of the Privy Council has my total support, for the executive must answer to the Canadian people not only for its actions but also for the organizations under its responsibility. Furthermore, if the decision is based on a false principle or false facts, it must be changed. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the minister and his cabinet do not intend to exercise that kind of control. It is not a posteriori but rather a priori control. Then, the minister is casting suspicion on the integrity and the objectivity of the Canadian Transport Commission. It is impossible for the decision of the commission not to be strongly influenced and for the adjudication to remain impartial.
In fact, by deciding to take over Nordair the Progressive Conservative government gets deeply involved in the decisional process. So, what is left to the Canadian Transport Commission whose exclusive jurisdiction in this matter is not questioned even by the minister? The commission is then placed in an impossible situation since it will have to establish who shall take over Nordair, when the Progressive Conservative govern-

ment has made its choice. Should the decision of the commission be different, it can be appealable to the governor in council where the initial decision was made in the first place.
Mr. Speaker, tonight I hope that I will get a supplementary answer to the questions I put and, particularly after having drawn those additional facts to the attention of the minister, that he will review his position and his conduct which I consider very dangerous.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-SALE OF NORDAIR-INQUIRY WHETHER QUESTION WILL BE REFERRED TO CTC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, naturally I can assure the hon. member that the final decision in this regard rests with the minister, with the cabinet, and with the government. In the meantime, on the question of the return of Nordair Limited to the private sector and the role of the Air Transport Committee of the Canadian Transport Commission, I want to assure the hon. member and the House that this government understands that this sale of Nordair shares now held by Air Canada is a matter subject to the full regulatory process. The Air Transport Committee has a role to play, pursuant to either part III of the Air Carrier Regulations, or section 27 of the National Transportation Act, depending upon who purchases Nordair. The Air Transport Committee has, and may exercise, full discretion to review the proposed sale with the full support of this government.
When an agreement of sale has been concluded, notice of the proposed transaction must be given to the Air Transport Committee, and in turn the committee would publish such notice. If objections are filed, a public hearing may be called. The committee then may disallow any proposed transaction if, in its opinion, such a transaction unduly restricts competition, or is otherwise prejudicial to the public interest.
Let me remind the hon. member that it was the former minister of transport in the previous government who was in power during the acquisition of Nordair Limited by Air Canada. It was also the former minister of transport who announced in November of last year that it was desirable to preserve the independent operations of Nordair from Air Canada, and it was the former minister of transport who instructed Air Canada to negotiate the sale of its Nordair shares with interested parties, and later instructed Transport Canada to take over these discussions.
This government, then, is completing a process it did not start. We are attempting to return Nordair to the private sector in a fair and orderly fashion, recognizing the real interests of the various parties involved. Any change in ownership in Nordair will naturally be subject to the full regulatory process of the Air Transport Committee of the Canadian Transport Commission at the appropriate time.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, let me reiterate, in respect of the hon. member's concern, that once a final decision is made it will naturally be up to the minister, the cabinet, and the government, to approve such decision.
November 29, 1979

subtopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-POSSIBLE PROSECUTIONS- ROLE OF TRANSPORT MINISTER IN DISCUSSION
COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-POSSIBLE PROSECUTIONS- ROLE OF TRANSPORT MINISTER IN DISCUSSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Thursday, October 18, 1 asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) if he or his department had taken any position on the advisability of proceeding with prosecutions in the Western Transport Association case. I also asked him if he would be prepared to table certain documents in respect of that particular matter. At that time the minister replied by saying, "the hon. member's allegations are absolute nonsense". On a supplementary question he allowed that he did ask a couple of questions, but that he "did not keep track of them".
Moments later, in reply to a question posed by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand), the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) indicated that the Minister of Transport was in attendance at the meeting because "the matter under consideration involved questions which were pertinent to matters of policy of the Department of Transport". Clearly there is an inconsistency here.
The Minister of Transport tells us that any suggestion that he might have taken an interest in the advisability of prosecution is absolute nonsense. Ele says he only asked a few questions, none of which he can remember. Yet the Prime Minister says that the Minister of Transport had a key interest in what happened at the meeting and that he was in attendance because the issues being raised were pertinent to his department.
This is not the only inconsistency which one finds when going over the record. The Solicitor General and Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Lawrence), when first asked whether the meeting had even taken place, informed this House that my sources were "completely and totally erroneous". When challenged again, he argued that the meeting was only one in a series of ongoing meetings. Four former ministers of consumer and corporate affairs have assured this House that no meeting of this nature has taken place in recent history. Yet the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has told this House that the meeting was one of a series of ongoing meetings.
Of course, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs cannot be accused of being consistent. First he told the House that there was no meeting, then he told the House that there was a meeting, but that it was only one in a series of meetings. That was on Friday. On Tuesday he told the House, "that this was the first time that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) had been to that type of meeting". He also said that no representations were received from the Minister of Transport.
By Wednesday, he was denying responsibility for the meetings altogether. He claimed that the meeting was called by the Minister of Justice and that he showed up at the designated time. He also stated that he had sent a brief to the Minister of Transport in advance of the meeting. Then came the absolute clincher. On Tuesday of the following week, in answer to a
Adjournment Debate
question put by the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais), the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs came up with yet another version. This time he said, "the Minister of Transport was involved in the meeting so we could obtain information from that particular minister about certain provincial government regulations and interference in the whole question". How interesting.
On Friday the minister denies that there was a meeting at all. On Tuesday he said that no representations were received from the Minister of Transport at this non-existent meeting. On Wednesday he denies any involvement, putting the blame squarely on the shoulders of a minister whom we cannot question because he is in the other place. On Thursday the Minister of Transport denies that he said anything at the meeting, but the Prime Minister quickly contradicts him. Then on the following Tuesday the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs says that the Minister of Transport was at the meeting to "make representations".
One would think, Mr. Speaker, that these gentlemen were tripping over themselves in an effort to contradict one another. Then, of course, we have the Minister of Justice in the other place. It would take far more time than I have here tonight to detail every time the Minister of Justice made a statement which directly contradicted what we were told in this House about the trucking affair. Needless to say, he took the basic position that the Minister of Transport was an active participant in the meeting and then said in effect, "so what?" He argued that as Attorney General he had every right to consult with whomever he pleased.
The issue I am raising here, Mr. Speaker, is not whether or not the Minister of Transport had the right to make recommendations or representations to the Attorney General. That is a complicated legal question, and there are positions on both sides. I am after something far more basic. I am after the facts. We have received in this House some very contradictory statements. We do not know whether to believe the Minister of Justice, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, the Minister of Transport, the Prime Minister, some of them or none of them. There has been a clear case of inconsistency here, to say the very least. We caught some gentlemen with their hands in the cookie jar so to speak, and they all blurted out different stories before they had a chance to get the story straight. Time has now passed and charges have in fact been laid.
I would ask the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jelinek) to give us the full facts of what happened at that meeting on Friday, October 12. I would further ask that the parliamentary secretary table the briefing document to which I referred in my question of October 18, in line with the spirit of open government and freedom of information-a topic about which there has been much discussion recently in this House. I would further ask that the parliamentary secretary table the minutes of that particular meeting so that any confusion that may exist, in the minds of those persons who participated, and outside that meeting may be laid to rest.

November 29, 1979
Adjournment Debate
I would conclude by pointing out that the one thing which none of the four cabinet ministers who have spoken on this matter have denied is that this meeting was in fact unprecedented, that this was the first time that there had been such a meeting involving cabinet ministers as well as a director of investigations and research. I would only point to the statement made by a former distinguished justice of the Supreme Court of Canada who said, "I would say that any consultation would have to be on the legal propriety of prosecution and not on any other elements. It might be, for instance, that some other members of cabinet may be very experienced in a particular branch of law involved; in which case he might consult them".
Finally, 1 would ask the parliamentary secretary to tell this House of the special expertise in this particular field which his minister, the Minister of Transport, brought to bear in considering whether or not the prosecution should proceed. Of course, there was in fact, a prosecution, but 1 believe the course of conduct over the whole history of this matter gives rise to many questions. I invite the parliamentary secretary to answer a few of them this evening.

speakeroldname: Mr. George Cooper (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-POSSIBLE PROSECUTIONS- ROLE OF TRANSPORT MINISTER IN DISCUSSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member has pointed out, this matter is sub judice. Accordingly, I have been asked to reply to the hon. member's statement.
On October 29 there was a very full inquiry by the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais) on this very subject. At that time I gave a reply which I hoped would put an end to this series of red herrings that has been dragged across the floor of the House on this issue. Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, I am surprised and disappointed that the hon. member would raise the matter again in the way he has. The questions he has raised are totally without merit.
1 want to make it absolutely clear, first of all, that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Flynn), or any other minister, is absolutely entitled, indeed required, to make whatever inquiries he deems fit in order to carry out his duties. Indeed he would be a fool if he did not make such inquiries. It is certainly true that he cannot be directed by anyone about how he should make up his mind in the case of a particular prosecution. He may seek advice, but he must make his own
decisions. I repeat, he not only may, but must, consult widely. He must consult his fellow cabinet ministers if he believes they can be of assistance in guiding him to a conclusion in a particular case.
The second point is that once the Minister of Justice has made his decision to prosecute, as he has in this case, then the matter is sub judice. By that I mean the matter is before the courts. At that point it is quite improper for any member of the House to comment on the advice the minister has received, or to ask questions on the matter. To do so would be to greatly disrupt the course of justice, or might result in that consequence. This is absolutely clear, even under the rules which apply under the freedom of information bill which we just referred to committee a few moments ago.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, when the court proceedings are over so that the sub judice rule is no longer applicable, any minister, or the Minister of Justice in this case, may be questioned in Parliament and may then be censured if Parliament agrees he has done something wrong.
What happened in this case is that the minister consulted with his cabinet colleagues, as was his right and duty. He laid charges on November 5 under the Combines Investigation Act, or caused his law officers to do so, as was his right and duty. Until these proceedings are settled in the courts, neither this minister nor any other minister will improperly divulge details of that advice, as is their right and duty.
If the hon. member believes that by moving forward to prosecute in this case the Minister of Justice has done something wrong-I cannot imagine how he could be seen to have done something wrong by deciding to prosecute-then let the hon. member intervene as he wishes, after the proceedings are over. In the meantime let him understand that his request is improper, that a reply would be improper, and that it is in the interests of this House, the people of Canada and the rule of law in this country, that justice take its course before the courts which is the proper place, and not on the floor of this Parliament.

The attached letter was sent to Deputy Heads of Government Departments and Agencies on Friday, November 23, 1979.
prime minister Ottawa, K1A 0A3
As you know, it is the firm intention of my colleagues and I to provide a more open government for Canada. The recent introduction of Freedom of Information legislation is an important step to this end, and I look forward to your co-operation to ensure that it will be effective in helping Canadians gain access to government records.
But as I indicated in speaking to Deputy Ministers some weeks ago, we can do much more to give the policy of open government full meaning and consistency. And we can act now in the spirit of the Freedom of Information legislation, even though it will be some time before its final form is established by Parliament and its administrative apparatus is in place.
One of the things we can do is to encourage open and responsive behaviour among public servants in their day to day dealings with the public, including particularly members of Parliament and representatives of the news media.
Ministers are responsible for the operations of government, and it is important to preserve the principle of ministerial responsibility. But within the framework, ministers must delegate many duties to public servants so that the operations of government can be carried out efficiently. Communications with the public are in this category, and ministers have now agreed formally by cabinet decision on guidelines for the participation of public servants in this respect.
These guidelines are attached. By this letter, I am asking you to arrange for their implementation in all branches of your department and in all regional operations as soon as possible.
It is for your decision which levels of public servants in your department are to be authorized to deal with the media. However, in the spirit of the guidelines, this list should be broad rather than narrow.
Finally, you may wish to arrange briefings by your professional media relations staff for officials subject to the guidelines in order to prepare them to meet their responsibilities.
Yours sincerely,
Joe Clark
POLICY GUIDELINES FOR PUBLIC SERVANTS: COMMUNICATIONS WITH THE PUBLIC
1.	Communications with the public, including particularly members of Parliament and news media representatives, are a part of the duties and responsibilities of managers in the public service. A staff function in support of this management role is performed by information officers in most departments and agencies.
2.	Public servants should be prepared to discuss frankly information within their areas of responsibility that describes or explains programs and policies that have been announced or implemented by the government.
3.	Public servants should not go beyond this discussion of factual information. It is not appropriate to discuss advice or recommendations tendered to ministers, or to speculate about policy deliberations or future policy decisions.
4.	It will be normal in many instances for public servants to be quoted by name, and to be interviewed for radio and television as well as by print media.
5.	These guidelines cannot and do not authorize the disclosure of information which is specifically prohibited by law. Public employees acting in good faith under these guidelines will not be considered as having violated their oaths or secrecy.
Friday, November 30, 1979
